Represent the reachable set as a bitset and the whole inner loop becomes `bits |= bits << n`, which processes 64 targets per machine word instead of one per iteration. That gives roughly a 64-fold constant-factor speedup with no change in asymptotic complexity. C# offers this through `System.Numerics.BigInteger` shifts or a hand-rolled `ulong[]`, and it is the standard trick for subset-sum problems where the target is large.

question: Unique paths in an m×n grid (only right/down moves).

followups.q: Why interleave the multiply and divide in the closed form?
followups.a: Because computing the full factorials first overflows almost immediately: 20 factorial already exceeds a signed 64-bit integer, so a 20x20 grid would fail even though its answer fits comfortably. Multiplying by one term and dividing by the next keeps the running value close to the final answer. The division is always exact at each step, since the product of any i consecutive integers is divisible by i factorial, which is the non-obvious fact that makes the loop safe.

followups.q: Suppose some cells are blocked.
followups.a: A blocked cell contributes zero paths, so set its value to 0 and carry on; everything downstream naturally accounts for it. The one trap is the start cell being blocked, which makes the answer 0 immediately and is easy to miss when initialising. The obstacle version is the more realistic problem, and it shows why the DP is worth knowing even though the clean grid has a closed form that the DP does not generalise to.

followups.q: Suppose diagonal moves were also allowed.
followups.a: Add the diagonal predecessor to the sum, so each cell becomes above plus left plus above-left. The counts grow much faster, which is worth flagging because overflow arrives sooner. Note the closed form disappears entirely: with three move types the paths are no longer a simple choice of positions among a fixed number of moves, so the DP is the only practical route. That is a neat demonstration that a formula is a special case while the DP is the general tool.

question: Minimum path sum in a grid.

followups.q: In the rolling row, how do you know row[c] still holds the value from above?
followups.a: Because the loop moves left to right and writes each cell after reading it. When computing column c, `row[c]` has not been touched yet in this row, so it is still the previous row's value, which is the cell above; `row[c-1]` was written a moment ago, so it is the current row's cell to the left. That read-before-write ordering is the whole trick, and reversing the loop direction would silently break it, which is a good thing to state rather than leave implicit.

followups.q: Suppose movement in all four directions were allowed, not just right and down.
followups.a: The DP collapses, because a cell could be reached from a cell you have not computed yet, so there is no valid evaluation order. It becomes a shortest-path problem on a graph with non-negative weights, which is Dijkstra with a priority queue, at O(rc log(rc)). This is the cleanest illustration of when a grid DP stops applying: DP needs a partial order on the subproblems, and free movement destroys it.

followups.q: Suppose some cells had negative values.
followups.a: With only right and down moves the DP still works, because the move set forbids revisiting a cell and so no negative cycle can form. If free movement were also allowed, negative values would break Dijkstra and you would need Bellman-Ford, and a negative cycle would mean no minimum exists at all. Pointing out that the answer depends on both the sign of the weights and the freedom of movement, rather than just one of them, is the strong version of this answer.

question: Best time to buy/sell stock with cooldown (or with transaction fee).

followups.q: Why capture the previous values into temporaries here, when the fee version updated in place?
followups.a: Because the cooldown transitions genuinely need yesterday's values: `free` must read yesterday's `sold`, and if `sold` were already updated to today's value the cooldown would be skipped entirely. In the fee version, using today's value corresponded to a same-day sell and rebuy, which was harmless. Here it would be wrong. That difference is worth stating precisely, because 'update in place' is a habit that silently breaks the moment a transition depends on a delayed state.

followups.q: Why is the answer the maximum of sold and free rather than just free?
followups.a: Because the final day might be a selling day, in which case the profit sits in `sold` and has not yet propagated into `free`, which only receives it on the following day. Returning `free` alone would miss a sale on the last day. Holding is excluded because ending the period still owning a share is never optimal: selling at any point cannot reduce the balance since prices are non-negative.

followups.q: Suppose the cooldown were k days rather than one.
followups.a: The single `free` variable becomes a window: the buy state must draw from the sell state of k+1 days earlier, so you keep a small ring buffer or an array of the last k sell values. It stays O(n) time and becomes O(k) space. The three-state machine generalises to a chain of k cooldown states, which is the same shape as extending the reorganize-string cooldown from one to k. Both problems are really 'delay a transition by k steps'.

question: Word break II: return all sentences from segmenting a string.

followups.q: Why run the boolean feasibility check when the memoised search would also return empty?
followups.a: Because the memoised search still has to explore before concluding nothing works, and on an adversarial input such as a long run of a single character with a dictionary that cannot cover it, that exploration is exponential even though the answer is empty. The boolean DP answers the same question in O(n squared) and short-circuits it. It is a good illustration that memoisation bounds repeated work but not the size of the search space, so a cheap precondition can still matter enormously.

followups.q: Can this problem ever be polynomial?
followups.a: No, because the output itself can be exponential: a string of n identical characters with a dictionary containing every prefix produces a number of segmentations growing exponentially in n. Any algorithm that must enumerate them is bounded below by the output size. That is why the counting version and the boolean version are polynomial while the enumeration version cannot be, and saying so explicitly is a stronger answer than trying to optimise it further.

followups.q: Why memoise by index rather than by the remaining substring?
followups.a: Because the index uniquely identifies the suffix and is a cheap integer key, whereas keying on the substring allocates a new string per lookup and hashes its whole length. For a long input that is a substantial constant-factor cost on every recursive call. Keying on position is the standard technique whenever the state is a suffix or prefix of a fixed input, and it applies equally to edit distance and longest common subsequence.

question: Longest palindromic subsequence.

followups.q: Why must the outer loop count downward?
followups.a: Because the recurrence reads `best[i + 1][...]`, a range starting one position later, so that value must already be computed. Iterating i upward would read uninitialised zeros and silently produce answers that are too small. Whenever a DP recurrence refers to a larger index, that loop runs in the opposite direction, which is the same rule that governs the palindrome-partitioning precomputation and the 0/1 knapsack capacity loop.

followups.q: How does this relate to the longest common subsequence?
followups.a: It is exactly the LCS of the string and its reverse, which is a satisfying equivalence: a palindromic subsequence reads the same forwards and backwards, so it is common to both. That gives an alternative implementation reusing an LCS routine, at the same O(n squared) cost. The direct interval DP is marginally cheaper since it needs one triangle rather than a full table, but the equivalence is worth knowing because it means improvements to one transfer to the other.

followups.q: What is the minimum number of insertions to make a string a palindrome?
followups.a: The length minus the longest palindromic subsequence. Every character not part of the longest palindromic subsequence needs a matching partner inserted, and that count is exactly the difference. It is a neat corollary that turns a second problem into a one-line derivation from this one, and the same subtraction gives the minimum deletions, since deleting the non-participating characters leaves a palindrome.

question: Decode ways (number of ways to decode a digit string).

followups.q: Why is 100 undecodable?
followups.a: The first zero pairs with the 1 to make 10, which is valid. The second zero then has a 0 before it, and 00 is not in the range 10 to 26, nor can a zero stand alone. So there is no way to consume it and the answer is 0. Solutions that handle only a leading zero pass '06' and fail '100', which is why both belong in the tests. The general rule is that a zero must always be the second digit of a 10 or a 20.

followups.q: Why return immediately when the count reaches zero?
followups.a: Because an undecodable position makes the whole string undecodable, and continuing would let a later position read a stale rolling value and produce a non-zero answer. It is also a genuine early exit rather than only a correctness guard. Writing the recurrence so that zeros propagate naturally also works, but the explicit return states the intent and avoids depending on multiplication-by-zero behaviour that a later edit could break.

followups.q: How does decode ways II with wildcards differ?
followups.a: A '*' can stand for any digit 1 to 9, so each term becomes a count of possibilities rather than a boolean: a single '*' contributes nine ways, and a pair involving a star contributes a count depending on which combinations fall in 10 to 26. The structure is identical but each branch multiplies by a factor, and the answer must be taken modulo a large prime because it grows enormously. It is a good illustration that the recurrence survives while the arithmetic inside it changes.

question: Maximal square: largest square of 1s in a binary matrix.

followups.q: Why the minimum of three neighbours rather than, say, the smaller of two?
followups.a: Because a square of side k at a corner requires a square of side k-1 to exist in all three directions simultaneously. Using only the cell above and to the left would allow an L-shaped region to be counted as a square: imagine a full row and a full column meeting at a corner with a hole in between. The diagonal neighbour is what certifies the interior is filled. Dropping it is the classic wrong answer and it passes every test case with no holes.

followups.q: Suppose it asked for the largest rectangle rather than the largest square.
followups.a: The DP does not generalise, because a rectangle has two independent dimensions and the min-of-three trick relies on a single one. The standard solution treats each row as the base of a histogram of consecutive 1s above it, then runs the largest-rectangle-in-a-histogram algorithm per row using a monotonic stack, giving O(rows x cols). It is a genuinely different technique, which is why interviewers sometimes ask the square first and the rectangle as the escalation.

followups.q: Why pad the table with an extra row and column?
followups.a: So that cells on the first row or column can read their neighbours without a boundary check. The padded zeros correctly represent 'no square beyond the edge', which is exactly the right value, so correctness and convenience agree. It costs one extra row and column of memory and removes four conditionals from the hot loop. The offset by one between matrix and table indices is the price, and it is the usual source of confusion when reading this kind of code.

question: Target sum: count ways to assign +/- to reach a target.

followups.q: Why does a zero in the input double the number of ways?
followups.a: Because a zero can take either sign without changing the sum, so every valid assignment of the other numbers yields two assignments overall. The DP handles it naturally, since adding zero to a reachable sum leaves it reachable and the count accumulates. It is worth testing explicitly because a solution that deduplicates subsets by value rather than by position would collapse those cases and undercount, which is the difference between counting subsets and counting assignments.

followups.q: Why must the loop over sums descend?
followups.a: So each number is used at most once. Descending, `ways[s - n]` still reflects counts built without the current number, because that lower index has not been updated in this pass. Ascending would let the same number contribute repeatedly, which answers the unbounded version of the problem instead. It is the identical loop-direction distinction as 0/1 versus unbounded knapsack, and it is a one-character change with completely different semantics.

followups.q: What if the numbers could be negative?
followups.a: The derivation breaks, because the subset sum could then be negative and an array indexed from zero cannot represent it. You would shift the index by the total to allow negative sums, doubling the table width, or use a dictionary keyed on the running sum. The problem statement usually restricts to non-negative values precisely so the clean transformation works, and noticing that the restriction is what enables the trick is the point of the follow-up.

question: Regular expression / wildcard matching with DP.

followups.q: How does this differ from regex matching with '.' and '*'?
followups.a: There the star binds to the character before it and means zero or more of *that* character, so the recurrence must look two columns back to skip the pair and must check the bound character before consuming input. Here the star is standalone and matches any sequence, so it looks one column back and one row up. That difference makes wildcard matching noticeably simpler, and it is why the two problems have different solutions despite looking similar.

followups.q: Is there a linear-time solution?
followups.a: Yes, a greedy two-pointer with backtracking on the last star. Advance both pointers while characters match; on a star, record its position and the input position and try matching nothing; on a mismatch, return to the last star and let it consume one more character. That is O(n) time and O(1) space in practice, though adversarial patterns with many stars can degrade. It is the harder solution to get right, so the DP is the safer interview answer with the greedy mentioned as the optimisation.

followups.q: Where is wildcard matching actually used?
followups.a: Shell globbing, file filters, and routing rules in gateways and firewalls. That last one matters for security: a rule like `/admin/*` matching more or less than intended is a real vulnerability class, and different implementations disagree about whether a star crosses a path separator. It is worth knowing that glob semantics are not standardised the way regex largely is, so a pattern that works in one system may match differently in another.

question: Number of longest increasing subsequences (count of LIS).

followups.q: Why replace the count on a strict improvement but add on a tie?
followups.a: Because a strictly longer subsequence invalidates everything recorded so far for that index: those shorter routes are no longer of maximal length, so their counts are irrelevant. A tie means another equally long route has been found, so both contribute and the counts sum. Reversing the two produces answers that are too large or too small in ways that pass on simple inputs, which is why [1,3,5,4,7] is the test to use: it has exactly two maximal subsequences and a wrong implementation typically reports one or three.

followups.q: Why does an array of equal values give a count equal to its length?
followups.a: Because the subsequence must be strictly increasing, so no two equal elements can both appear, and every maximal subsequence has length one. There are five positions, hence five distinct subsequences of that length. It is a useful test because it exercises the case where the longest length is the initial value and no inner loop iteration ever fires, which a solution that only accumulates during extension would get wrong.

followups.q: Can this be done in O(n log n) like plain LIS?
followups.a: Yes, but it is considerably harder. The patience-sorting approach keeps piles of tails; counting requires each pile to store prefix sums of counts so that the number of ways to reach a given length can be queried by binary search. The result is O(n log n) with substantially more code and more room for error. For interview purposes the quadratic version with a correct replace-versus-accumulate rule is the expected answer, and naming the faster one shows you know the ceiling.

question: Generate all subsets (the power set).

followups.q: Why copy current into a new list rather than adding it directly?
followups.a: Because `current` is a single mutable list that the recursion keeps changing. Adding it by reference would put the same object into the result eight times, and every entry would end up showing whatever state it held at the end, typically empty. It is the classic aliasing bug in backtracking, and it produces output that is uniformly wrong rather than subtly wrong, which at least makes it easy to spot. The copy is what makes each recorded subset a snapshot.

followups.q: Suppose the input contains duplicates and subsets must be unique.
followups.a: Sort first, then in the loop skip any element equal to the previous one at the same recursion depth, using `if (i > index && nums[i] == nums[i-1]) continue;`. Sorting puts equal values adjacent so the check is local, and the `i > index` part is essential: it allows a duplicate to be used at a deeper level, where it legitimately extends a subset, while preventing it from starting a second identical branch at the same level. Getting that condition wrong either produces duplicates or drops valid subsets.

followups.q: When would you choose the bitmask version?
followups.a: When n is at most about 20 to 30 and you want iteration without recursion, which avoids stack depth and is easier to parallelise since each mask is independent. It is also the natural representation for bitmask DP, where a subset is a state, as in the travelling salesman DP. The limit is real though: at n = 31 the shift overflows a signed int, and the enumeration itself is already astronomically large well before that, so in practice n is small whenever this approach applies at all.

question: Generate all permutations of a list.

followups.q: Explain the duplicate-skipping condition, especially the !used[i-1] part.
followups.a: After sorting, equal values are adjacent. The rule is that among a run of identical values, they must be used left to right; picking a later duplicate while its identical predecessor is still unused would generate a permutation already produced by the mirror choice. So `!used[i-1]` detects exactly that situation and prunes it. Writing `used[i-1]` instead inverts the logic and drops valid permutations, which is the standard mistake. The condition is small and the reasoning is not, so it is worth deriving on a [1,1,2] example rather than reciting.

followups.q: Suppose you need the next permutation in lexicographic order rather than all of them.
followups.a: That is a different, much cheaper algorithm: scan from the right for the first element smaller than its successor, find the rightmost element greater than it, swap them, then reverse the suffix. It is O(n) time and O(1) space, and it is what `std::next_permutation` does. When you only need to iterate permutations one at a time, or when n is large enough that n! is out of the question, generating the next one on demand is the right tool.

followups.q: How does the swap-based version differ, and why might you avoid it?
followups.a: It permutes the array in place by swapping the current index with each later index, which avoids the `used` array and the per-level allocation. It is slightly faster, but it destroys the relative order of the remaining elements, so the output is not lexicographic even for sorted input, and the duplicate-skipping trick no longer works because equal values are no longer reliably adjacent. For the unique-permutations variant the `used` array version is the one to reach for.

question: Combination sum: find combinations that sum to a target (reuse allowed).

followups.q: Why does passing i rather than i + 1 give reuse, and why not pass 0?
followups.a: Passing `i` lets the current candidate be chosen again at the next level, which is the reuse the problem wants. Passing `0` would also allow reuse but would additionally revisit earlier candidates, generating [2,3] and [3,2] as separate results. Starting at `i` forces every combination to be built in non-decreasing order, so each multiset is produced exactly once. That is the same ordering trick that makes the coin-change combination count work, seen from the enumeration side.

followups.q: Why break rather than continue when the candidate overshoots?
followups.a: Because the array is sorted, so if candidates[i] already exceeds the remaining target, every candidate after it exceeds it too and the rest of the loop is guaranteed to be fruitless. `continue` would test each of them individually, which is correct but wasteful. On inputs with many large candidates the difference is substantial, and it is the main reason to sort at all here, since sorting is not needed for correctness.

followups.q: Suppose each candidate may be used at most once, and the input contains duplicates.
followups.a: That is Combination Sum II, and it needs two changes: recurse with `i + 1` so each element is consumed, and skip duplicates at the same level with `if (i > start && candidates[i] == candidates[i-1]) continue;`. The `i > start` guard is what distinguishes 'this is a repeat of a sibling choice' from 'this is a legitimate second copy deeper in the tree'. It is the same pruning condition as in subsets-with-duplicates, which is worth pointing out as the shared pattern.

question: Combinations: choose k numbers from 1..n.

followups.q: Explain the pruning bound n - needed + 1.
followups.a: If `needed` more numbers must be chosen and all must be strictly greater than the current one, the largest possible starting value is n - needed + 1, because anything higher leaves fewer than needed values above it. Looping past that point explores branches guaranteed to fail. For n of 20 and k of 10 it removes a substantial fraction of the search. It is the same class of bound as breaking out of a sorted candidate loop in combination sum: cheap arithmetic that eliminates provably dead subtrees.

followups.q: How does this differ from generating permutations?
followups.a: Permutations recurse from index zero every time with a used-flags array, so order matters and [1,2] and [2,1] are distinct. Combinations recurse from i+1, which enforces strictly increasing order and makes each set appear once. That single difference in the recursive call is what separates n! outputs from n choose k, and being able to point at the exact line is a better answer than describing the concepts.

followups.q: Suppose you needed the combinations of an arbitrary list rather than 1..n, with duplicates.
followups.a: Sort the list first, then use index-based recursion as here, adding a skip for a value equal to the previous one at the same level: `if (i > start && items[i] == items[i-1]) continue;`. Sorting makes equal values adjacent so the check is local, and the `i > start` guard permits a duplicate deeper in the tree while preventing a repeated sibling branch. It is the identical pruning condition as in subsets-with-duplicates.

question: N-Queens: place N queens so none attack each other.

followups.q: Why do row - col and row + col identify the diagonals?
followups.a: Moving one step down-right increases both row and column by one, so their difference is unchanged along that diagonal. Moving down-left increases the row and decreases the column, so their sum is unchanged. That gives each diagonal a constant identifier, turning an O(n) scan along the diagonal into an O(1) array lookup. Adding n to the difference shifts the range from -(n-1)..(n-1) into 0..2n-2 so it can index an array, which is the only reason the offset is there.

followups.q: Suppose you only need the count, not the boards.
followups.a: Drop the rendering and the placement array, and the natural optimisation is a bitmask version: hold the three conflict sets as integers and use bit operations to compute all available columns at once, picking the lowest set bit each time. That removes the loop's repeated checks and is dramatically faster, comfortably handling n = 15 or so. Beyond that the count grows too fast for exhaustive search regardless of constant factors, and the known values come from specialised methods.

followups.q: Why are n = 2 and n = 3 impossible?
followups.a: For n = 2, one queen on a 2x2 board attacks every remaining square. For n = 3, wherever the first queen goes, the remaining rows cannot both be filled without a diagonal or column conflict; exhausting the nine placements shows it. Solutions exist for n = 1 and for every n of 4 or more. It is worth stating because a candidate who only tests n = 8 may write code that silently mishandles the no-solution case, and returning an empty list rather than throwing is the right behaviour.

followups.q: How would you exploit the board's symmetry?
followups.a: Solutions come in symmetry classes under the eight rotations and reflections of the square, so you can restrict the first queen to the left half of the first row and mirror the results, roughly halving the search. Full exploitation means canonicalising each solution under the symmetry group and expanding at the end, which is how published counts are computed efficiently. It is a good example of cutting a search by exploiting problem structure rather than by micro-optimising the inner loop.

question: Sudoku solver.

followups.q: Why bitmasks rather than scanning the row, column and box?
followups.a: Because scanning costs 27 comparisons per candidate digit per cell, and the search tries many candidates at many cells, so that constant multiplies through the whole exponential search. A bitmask makes the test three AND operations and the update three ORs, all constant. On a hard puzzle that difference is seconds versus milliseconds. It is a good example of an optimisation that does not change the complexity class but changes whether the program is usable.

followups.q: What is the single biggest further speedup?
followups.a: Choosing the most constrained cell rather than the next empty one - the minimum-remaining-values heuristic. Filling a cell with only one legal digit first prunes enormously, whereas filling in scan order explores branches that a later constraint would have eliminated. It costs a scan to find the best cell but typically reduces the search tree by orders of magnitude on hard puzzles. Constraint propagation, deducing forced digits before branching at all, is the next step and is what makes solvers instantaneous.

followups.q: Why does the test verify the solution rather than comparing to a known answer?
followups.a: Because a puzzle can have more than one solution unless it is well-formed, so asserting one exact grid would be fragile. Checking that every row, column and box contains all nine digits - which is what comparing against 0x1FF does - validates any correct answer. It is the same property-assertion approach used for reorganize-string and find-peak, and it also catches a solver that fills the grid without respecting the original givens.

followups.q: Why must the givens be validated before searching?
followups.a: Because the mask seeding is idempotent: setting the same bit twice looks identical to setting it once, so a board with two 5s in a row produces exactly the mask a legal board would. The solver then treats the position as valid and searches the remaining empty cells, which for a nearly empty board is an enormous space it may never exhaust. The symptom is not a wrong answer but a hang, which is far worse. Checking each given against the masks as they are seeded turns it into an immediate false.

question: Letter combinations of a phone number.

followups.q: Why must the empty input return an empty list rather than a list with one empty string?
followups.a: Because mathematically there is exactly one function from an empty set, so the product is arguably a single empty combination, but the problem statement specifies an empty result and callers expect that. It matters more than it sounds: the recursion naturally produces the single empty string, so you have to guard against it explicitly. That mismatch between the mathematically natural answer and the specified one is worth confirming rather than assuming, and it is the single most common way this easy problem is failed.

followups.q: Would you write this iteratively instead?
followups.a: You can, and it is clean: start with a list containing one empty string, then for each digit replace the list with every existing prefix extended by every letter for that digit. It is a breadth-first construction rather than depth-first, needs no recursion, and is easy to read. The trade-off is memory: it materialises every intermediate level, so at the last digit it holds the full result plus the previous level, whereas backtracking holds only one path at a time.

followups.q: Suppose this fed a real autocomplete over a dictionary, not just raw combinations.
followups.a: Then generating all combinations first is wasteful, since almost all of them are not words. Instead walk a trie of the dictionary in lockstep with the digits: at each digit, extend only those trie nodes that have a child for one of that digit's letters, pruning dead branches immediately. That is how T9 predictive text worked, and it turns an exponential enumeration into a search bounded by the number of real words sharing that prefix.

question: Generate valid parentheses combinations of n pairs.

followups.q: How many results are there, and why does that number appear so often?
followups.a: The nth Catalan number: 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 for n = 1 to 5. It counts balanced bracket sequences, and also the number of distinct binary search trees on n nodes, the triangulations of a polygon, and the ways to parenthesise a product. They are all the same counting problem in disguise, which is why 'count unique BSTs' and this question have identical answers. Recognising the sequence is a good signal that you have seen the structure before.

followups.q: Why is this considered better than generate-and-filter?
followups.a: Because the constraints are applied during construction rather than afterwards, so invalid branches are never explored. For n = 3, filtering would examine 64 strings to keep 5; the constrained search touches only the nodes leading to valid results. The saving grows exponentially with n. It is the defining characteristic of backtracking as opposed to brute-force enumeration: prune as early as the constraint can be evaluated, not at the leaves.

followups.q: Suppose there were multiple bracket types, as in a real expression.
followups.a: The single open-count no longer suffices, because closing must match the most recent unclosed opener, so you carry a stack of open types instead. You may open any type at any time while budget remains, and may close only the type on top of the stack. The count grows much faster since each opening choice multiplies the branching. That variant is closer to generating syntactically valid expressions, and it is a natural escalation for a candidate who solves the single-type version quickly.

question: Word search in a grid (single word).

followups.q: Why restore the cell rather than keep a visited set for the whole search?
followups.a: Because the exclusion is per path, not global. A cell used by one candidate path must remain available to a different path starting elsewhere, so a permanent visited marker would wrongly reject valid words. This is the defining difference between backtracking and flood fill: flood fill marks permanently because it is partitioning the grid, whereas here the grid is a search space each path traverses independently.

followups.q: Suppose you must find many words in the same grid, not one.
followups.a: Running this per word is O(words x rc x 4^L), which is far too slow. The right answer is Word Search II: build a trie of all the words, then do a single DFS from each cell walking the trie in lockstep with the grid, so a path is abandoned the moment no word continues with that prefix. One traversal finds every word, and pruning completed words from the trie keeps it shrinking. That is a standard escalation once a candidate solves the single-word version.

followups.q: Using '\0' as the marker mutates the caller's board. Is that acceptable?
followups.a: It is restored before returning, so the board is unchanged on exit, and it avoids allocating a visited grid. But it is not exception-safe: if anything threw mid-search the board would be left corrupted, and it is not thread-safe, since two concurrent searches would see each other's markers. For an interview it is the expected answer; for shared or concurrent code I would use a separate visited array and say so. The marker also assumes '\0' never appears as real data, which is the usual in-band sentinel caveat.

question: Palindrome partitioning: all ways to split into palindromes.

followups.q: Why is the count 16 for a five-character string of identical letters?
followups.a: Because every single character is a palindrome, so every possible set of cut positions is valid, and with n characters there are n-1 possible cut points each independently taken or not: 2^(n-1), which is 16 for n of 5. That is the worst case and it is exponential, which proves no polynomial algorithm can exist for enumerating all partitions. It is the same argument as for word break II, and stating it is more valuable than trying to optimise further.

followups.q: Why must the precomputation loop start from the end?
followups.a: Because isPalindrome[start, end] depends on isPalindrome[start + 1, end - 1], a range starting one position later, which must already be computed. Iterating start upward reads uninitialised false values and silently misses palindromes, giving too few partitions rather than an error. The rule is general: when a recurrence refers to a larger index, that loop runs in the opposite direction.

followups.q: What changes if only the minimum number of cuts is wanted?
followups.a: It becomes a one-dimensional DP rather than an enumeration: cuts[i] is the fewest cuts for the first i characters, computed as the best over every j where j..i is a palindrome. That is O(n squared) total and polynomial, because you are counting rather than listing. The contrast is worth drawing explicitly: the same precomputed table serves both, but one problem is tractable and the other cannot be, purely because of output size.

question: Restore IP addresses from a digit string.

followups.q: Why is the leading-zero rule necessary?
followups.a: Because IPv4 notation is not merely numeric: '01' and '1' are different strings and only the second is a valid segment. Historically some parsers treated a leading zero as octal, so '010' meant 8, which is a genuine source of security bugs where a blocklist and a resolver disagree about what an address means. The test with '0000' pins it down: without the rule it would produce several answers, and with it exactly one.

followups.q: What do the length checks actually save?
followups.a: They eliminate whole branches before recursing. A string of twelve digits with one segment placed leaves eleven digits for three segments, which cannot fit, so that branch is dead and worth rejecting immediately rather than discovering it four levels down. The outer check on total length rejects impossible inputs in constant time. Neither changes correctness, and on longer inputs they remove most of the search tree, which is the usual value of arithmetic pruning in backtracking.

followups.q: How would this change for IPv6?
followups.a: Eight groups of up to four hexadecimal digits, so the segment rules change and the search widens considerably. The harder part is the double-colon abbreviation, which represents a run of zero groups and may appear at most once, so the number of groups is no longer fixed and the parser must infer how many zeros the abbreviation stands for. That ambiguity is why IPv6 parsing is substantially harder than IPv4 and why it is usually left to a library.

question: Burst balloons (interval DP).

followups.q: Why does thinking about the first balloon fail?
followups.a: Because bursting a balloon joins its two neighbours, so the remaining array is not a simple subarray of the original and the left and right parts are no longer independent - a later burst on the left can be adjacent to something that was originally on the right. Subproblems must be independent for DP to apply. Choosing the last balloon instead fixes its neighbours as the untouched range boundaries, which restores independence. That inversion is the entire insight of the problem.

followups.q: Why pad the array with 1s?
followups.a: So that balloons at the ends have neighbours and the multiplication needs no special case. A missing neighbour is treated as 1, which is the multiplicative identity and therefore exactly the right value. It is the same technique as a dummy head node in a linked list or a sentinel row in a DP table: add an artificial element so the general rule covers the boundary. Without it every coin calculation would need two conditionals.

followups.q: Why iterate by increasing width rather than by index?
followups.a: Because the recurrence reads best[left, last] and best[last, right], both of which are strictly narrower ranges. Solving by widening width guarantees they are computed before they are read. Iterating by left and right directly in the obvious nested order would read uninitialised zeros and silently produce answers that are too small. Whenever an interval DP composes from sub-intervals, width is the loop that must be outermost.

question: Jump game: can you reach the last index?

followups.q: Why is greedy provably correct here, when it fails for so many other problems?
followups.a: Because reachability is monotonic and downward closed: if index j is reachable then every index before it is too, since jumps of any length up to nums[i] are allowed. So the set of reachable positions is always a prefix, and a single number, its furthest extent, describes it completely. There is no choice to regret, which is exactly the condition greedy needs. Contrast house robber, where taking a house forbids its neighbour, so the reachable set is not a simple prefix and greedy breaks.

followups.q: Suppose you also needed the minimum number of jumps.
followups.a: That is Jump Game II, still greedy but with more bookkeeping. Track the end of the current jump's range and the furthest reachable within it; when the scan reaches the end of the current range, a jump has been spent and the range extends to the furthest. It is O(n), essentially a BFS by levels where each level is one jump. The neat framing is that the greedy is really a breadth-first search that never needs a queue because the frontier is always a contiguous range.

followups.q: Suppose jumps could go backwards as well as forwards.
followups.a: The prefix property is destroyed, so greedy no longer applies and it becomes a genuine graph reachability problem, solved with BFS or DFS over positions in O(n) with a visited set. That is the 'jump game III' variant. It is a good illustration of how a small relaxation of the rules moves a problem from a two-line greedy to a standard traversal, and recognising which structural property the greedy depended on is what lets you spot that quickly.

question: Jump game II: minimum jumps to reach the end.

followups.q: Why does the loop stop before the last index?
followups.a: Because the jump that lands on the last index is counted when the range containing its predecessor is exhausted, not when you arrive. Including the final index would trigger one extra range exhaustion and return one jump too many for inputs where the last index happens to be a range boundary. It is the classic off-by-one in this problem, and the `[1,2]` test case exposes it: the answer is 1, and a loop running to the end returns 2.

followups.q: In what sense is this really a BFS?
followups.a: Each 'level' of the BFS is the set of indices reachable in exactly k jumps, and because jumps can be any length up to the value at a position, that set is always a contiguous range. A normal BFS would hold those indices in a queue; here the range is fully described by its two endpoints, so the queue collapses to two integers. Seeing that a BFS frontier is an interval, and therefore compressible, is the insight that turns an O(n) space algorithm into an O(1) one.

followups.q: Suppose some positions were unreachable, so the end could not be reached at all.
followups.a: This version assumes reachability, which the problem statement usually guarantees, and would return a wrong count rather than reporting failure. The fix is to check whether `furthest` ever fails to advance past the current index, exactly as Jump Game I does, and return -1 in that case. It is the same pattern as Boyer-Moore needing a verification pass: an algorithm that assumes a precondition should either check it or document that it does not.

question: Perfect squares: fewest perfect squares summing to n.

followups.q: Is there a mathematical shortcut?
followups.a: Yes. Lagrange's four-square theorem guarantees the answer is at most four. Legendre's three-square theorem says it is exactly four precisely when n has the form 4^a times (8b + 7). So you can test for a perfect square, then for a sum of two squares in O(sqrt n), then apply the Legendre test, and otherwise answer three. That is O(sqrt n) overall, far better than the DP. It is a legitimate answer but relies on number theory rather than algorithm design, which is why the DP remains the expected one.

followups.q: Why initialise to i rather than to int.MaxValue?
followups.a: Because i is a genuine upper bound, being i copies of one, so the minimum is always correct. It also avoids the overflow hazard of adding one to int.MaxValue, which would wrap to a large negative and win every comparison. That is the same trap as in coin change, where a MaxValue sentinel must be guarded explicitly. Choosing a real achievable bound rather than an infinity sentinel removes the problem rather than working around it.

followups.q: Could BFS solve this?
followups.a: Yes, and it is a nice alternative framing: treat each remaining value as a node, with an edge for subtracting each square, and find the shortest path from n to zero. BFS levels correspond to the number of squares used, so the first time zero is reached gives the answer. It has the advantage of stopping early rather than filling a whole table, which matters when the answer is small, and since the theorems above guarantee at most four levels, BFS terminates very quickly in practice.

question: Longest arithmetic subsequence.

followups.q: Why a dictionary per index rather than a two-dimensional array?
followups.a: Because the common difference ranges over all integers, including negatives, so it cannot index an array directly without offsetting by the value range, which for large values is impractical. A dictionary keyed on the difference stores only the differences that actually occur, which is at most n per index. If the value range were small and known, an offset array would be faster by avoiding hashing, and that is a reasonable optimisation to mention when the constraints allow it.

followups.q: Why is the base length 2 rather than 1?
followups.a: Because any two elements form an arithmetic sequence by definition - the difference between them is the common difference. So the first time a difference is seen between j and i, the run is already length 2, not 1. Starting at 1 would undercount every result by one. It also means the answer for any array of two or more elements is at least 2, which is why the short-array case returns the length directly.

followups.q: Does this handle a common difference of zero?
followups.a: Yes, and the all-sevens test confirms it: the difference is 0 and each element extends the run, giving 4. That case is worth testing because a solution using the difference as an array index with an offset can mishandle zero, and because some implementations special-case duplicates unnecessarily. Here it needs no special handling at all, which is a sign the abstraction is right.

question: Distinct subsequences: count subsequences of s equal to t.

followups.q: Why must the inner loop run backwards?
followups.a: Because with a single row, `ways[j - 1]` must still hold the previous row's value when it is read. Iterating forwards would have already updated it for the current character, so a single character of s could be counted twice in one pass. It is the same loop-direction rule as 0/1 versus unbounded knapsack: descending means each item contributes once. Getting it wrong gives counts that are too large on inputs with repeated characters, which is exactly what 'aaaa' against 'aa' exposes.

followups.q: Why does aaaa against aa give 6?
followups.a: Because it is choosing 2 positions from 4, which is 6 combinations, and every choice yields the same string but a distinct subsequence by position. That is the definition the problem uses: subsequences are counted by the positions selected, not by the resulting text. If distinct strings were wanted, the answer would be 1. Clarifying which definition applies is worth doing before writing anything, since the two produce wildly different numbers.

followups.q: Why return long?
followups.a: Because the count grows combinatorially and overflows a 32-bit int quickly: a string of thirty identical characters with a target of fifteen already exceeds int range. The problem statements that keep it in int do so by constraining the input, which is a habit worth not absorbing. Where the count can be enormous, the usual real-world answer is to compute it modulo a large prime, which is what competitive problems specify for exactly this reason.

question: Binary search: find a target in a sorted array.

followups.q: Why is the overflow in (low + high) / 2 not theoretical?
followups.a: It was a real bug in Java's standard library for nine years, and in the binary search that Jon Bentley published and that was widely copied. With arrays near two billion elements the sum exceeds int.MaxValue and wraps negative, producing a negative index and an exception. It needs a genuinely huge array to trigger, which is exactly why it survived so long in code everyone believed was correct. Writing `low + (high - low) / 2` costs nothing and removes the class of bug.

followups.q: How do you find the first and last occurrence of a duplicated target?
followups.a: Use the lower-bound form twice. The first occurrence is the lower bound of the target; the last is the lower bound of target + 1, minus one. The key change from the plain search is that on an equal comparison you do not return, you keep narrowing toward the side you want. Trying to bolt a linear scan onto a plain binary search once a match is found ruins the complexity: on an array that is entirely the target, that degrades to O(n).

followups.q: What is 'binary search on the answer'?
followups.a: Searching over a range of candidate answers rather than over array indices, valid whenever the predicate is monotonic: if a capacity of 10 works, so does 11. Koko eating bananas, splitting an array to minimise the largest sum, and the minimum ship capacity in D days are all this. You binary search the answer space and use a linear feasibility check as the comparison, giving O(n log(range)). Spotting that a problem has a monotonic predicate is the actual skill being tested.

question: Search a 2D matrix (rows and columns sorted).

followups.q: Why start at the top-right rather than the top-left?
followups.a: Because the top-right is the only corner where the two directions disagree: moving left strictly decreases and moving down strictly increases, so every comparison eliminates an entire row or column. From the top-left both directions increase, so a value smaller than the target gives no information about which way to go, and you would have to explore both. The bottom-left works equally well by symmetry. Recognising that the corner choice is what makes the elimination unambiguous is the substance of this question.

followups.q: Could you binary search the staircase version to beat O(rows + cols)?
followups.a: Not in general. You can binary search each row for O(rows log cols), which is worse than O(rows + cols) for square matrices and better for very wide ones, so it depends on the shape. There is a divide-and-conquer approach achieving roughly O(n^1.58) for an n by n matrix, but the staircase is linear in the perimeter and far simpler. For a square matrix O(rows + cols) is optimal, since an adversary can arrange the target to require examining one element per diagonal.

followups.q: Suppose the matrix were enormous and stored across pages or disk blocks.
followups.a: Then the access pattern matters more than the comparison count. The staircase walks one row and one column, which is poor locality for a row-major layout, since each column step jumps a full row stride. The flattened binary search is also scattered but touches far fewer elements. In practice you would either store a per-row min and max to skip whole rows cheaply, or use a structure designed for the access pattern such as a space-filling-curve layout, which is the kind of consideration that separates the interview answer from the production one.

question: Find minimum in a rotated sorted array.

followups.q: Why compare against the right end rather than the left?
followups.a: Because the right comparison distinguishes the two halves unambiguously. In a rotated array every element in the left segment is greater than every element in the right segment, so if the midpoint exceeds the rightmost value the rotation point must be to its right. Comparing against the left fails on an unrotated array, where the midpoint is greater than the leftmost yet the minimum is at index 0, so you would need an extra check for that case. Choosing the right end removes the special case entirely.

followups.q: Why high = mid rather than mid - 1?
followups.a: Because when the midpoint is not greater than the rightmost value, the midpoint itself may be the minimum, so excluding it could discard the answer. That is the same asymmetry as in a lower-bound search: one side advances past the midpoint, the other converges onto it. Writing `mid - 1` on that branch produces a function that is correct on most inputs and wrong when the minimum lands exactly on a midpoint, which is a miserable bug to reproduce.

followups.q: Why can duplicates not be handled in logarithmic time?
followups.a: Because when the midpoint, the left and the right values are all equal, no information distinguishes the halves: the array could be [2,2,2,0,2] or [2,0,2,2,2] and both look identical at those three positions. The only safe move is to shrink the range by one, which in the worst case of an all-equal array gives O(n). No algorithm can do better, since an adversary can hide the minimum behind indistinguishable values, so the degradation is inherent rather than an implementation weakness.

question: Koko eating bananas / capacity to ship in D days (binary search on the answer).

followups.q: How do you recognise a 'binary search on the answer' problem?
followups.a: Three signals together. The question asks for a minimum or maximum value rather than a position; checking whether a specific candidate works is straightforward, usually a linear pass; and feasibility is monotonic, so if a candidate works then every larger one does too, or every smaller one for a maximisation. When those hold, you binary search the answer range and use the check as the comparison. Splitting an array to minimise the largest subarray sum, and the minimum ship capacity above, are the same shape wearing different words.

followups.q: Why must the lower bound be the largest single element rather than one?
followups.a: For the shipping problem, because a package cannot be split across ships, so any capacity below the heaviest package is infeasible no matter how many days are available, and the feasibility check would loop forever or report an impossible result. Starting at the maximum makes every candidate in the range at least potentially valid, which is what keeps the monotonic predicate well defined. Koko differs because a pile can be eaten over several hours, so a speed of one is always feasible given enough time.

followups.q: Why the (p + speed - 1) / speed idiom?
followups.a: It is integer ceiling division: eating a pile of 7 at speed 3 takes three hours, not two, because the final hour is partly idle. Writing `p / speed` truncates and understates the time, which makes an infeasible speed look feasible and produces an answer that is too small. The alternative is `Math.Ceiling` with floating point, which I would avoid here since it introduces precision concerns into what is exact integer arithmetic.

followups.q: Suppose the feasibility check itself were expensive, say a database query.
followups.a: Then the O(log range) factor matters a great deal, and you would want to narrow the range first with cheap bounds or a coarse estimate before binary searching, and cache results since the same candidate may be revisited across runs. If the check were also noisy or non-deterministic, monotonicity could fail and binary search would become unsafe, at which point you need a different strategy entirely. Naming that dependency on a reliable, monotonic predicate is the mature version of this answer.

question: Find the square root of an integer (without built-in).

followups.q: Why compare with division instead of computing mid * mid?
followups.a: Because the product overflows. For n near int.MaxValue the candidate root approaches 46,341, and squaring that exceeds int range, wrapping to a negative number so the comparison takes the wrong branch and the search diverges. Widening to long fixes it, but the division form avoids the problem entirely without a wider type, which matters in languages or contexts where the wider type is unavailable. The 2147395599 test exists precisely to catch the naive version.

followups.q: When would Newton's method be the better choice?
followups.a: When the input is large or the root must be computed to many digits, because Newton's converges quadratically, roughly doubling the correct digits each iteration, against one bit per iteration for binary search. For 32-bit integers it takes a handful of steps against about 16, which is a real but modest saving. Its downsides are needing a sensible starting guess and behaving badly at zero, and for integer arithmetic the termination condition needs care to avoid oscillating between two adjacent values.

followups.q: Why return high rather than low at the end?
followups.a: Because when the loop exits without an exact match, `high` is the largest candidate whose square does not exceed n and `low` has moved one past it, so `high` is the floor of the true root. The pointers cross by exactly one, which is the invariant to state. Returning `low` gives the ceiling, and mixing them up produces an answer that is right for perfect squares and off by one for everything else, which the `MySqrt(8)` test catches immediately.

question: Explain and implement quicksort.

followups.q: Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but O(n^2) worst case, while merge sort is always O(n log n). Why is quicksort still used?
followups.a: Constants and memory. Quicksort sorts in place with excellent cache locality, since partitioning is a sequential scan, whereas merge sort needs O(n) auxiliary space and copies between buffers. In practice quicksort is typically two to three times faster on arrays despite the worse bound. The worst case is also avoidable: randomised pivots make it improbable, and introsort, which is what most standard libraries ship, monitors recursion depth and switches to heapsort if it degrades, giving a hard O(n log n) guarantee with quicksort's speed.

followups.q: What happens on an array with many duplicate values?
followups.a: This two-way partition degrades badly: with all elements equal, every partition puts everything on one side and the recursion is quadratic. The fix is three-way partitioning, the Dutch national flag scheme, which groups elements less than, equal to and greater than the pivot, so all the duplicates are placed in one step and never recursed into. That turns the all-equal case from the worst input into the best one, which is why the sort-colors problem is really teaching a quicksort component.

followups.q: Why is quicksort not stable, and when does that matter?
followups.a: Because partitioning swaps elements across long distances, so two equal elements can have their relative order reversed. It matters when sorting by successive keys, for instance ordering by department and then expecting ties to remain in the original order, which is exactly what LINQ's `OrderBy` then `ThenBy` relies on. That is why `OrderBy` uses a stable merge sort while `Array.Sort` uses unstable introsort, and choosing the wrong one produces bugs that are invisible until the data happens to contain ties.

question: Explain and implement merge sort.

followups.q: Exactly which line makes it stable, and why?
followups.a: The final `else`, which takes from the left half when the two front elements are equal. The left half holds elements that came earlier in the original array, so preferring it preserves their relative order. Changing that comparison from strictly-less to less-or-equal on the right side would silently make the sort unstable while still producing correctly ordered output, which is a bug that only manifests when sorting by a secondary key. It is one character, and it is the whole stability guarantee.

followups.q: Why sort data larger than memory with merge sort rather than quicksort?
followups.a: Because merging is purely sequential: it reads two runs front to back and writes one output stream, which is ideal for disk or network where sequential throughput vastly exceeds random access. Quicksort's partitioning jumps around the array, which is fine in RAM and disastrous on disk. External merge sort splits the data into memory-sized runs, sorts each, then merges them in passes, which is exactly how databases perform large ORDER BY operations and how the merge-k-sorted-lists problem generalises.

followups.q: What does the nums[mid] <= nums[mid + 1] check buy you?
followups.a: It skips the merge when the two halves are already in order, which makes an already-sorted array O(n) instead of O(n log n) and helps substantially on partially sorted real-world data. It costs one comparison per merge. That idea taken further is the basis of TimSort, which detects existing sorted runs and merges them, and is why sorting nearly-sorted data in Python or Java is dramatically faster than the theoretical bound suggests.

question: Quickselect: find the kth smallest/largest in average O(n).

followups.q: Why is the average O(n) rather than O(n log n)?
followups.a: Because only one side is recursed into. Quicksort solves both halves, giving T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n), which is O(n log n). Quickselect gives T(n) = T(n/2) + O(n), and that geometric series n + n/2 + n/4 + ... sums to 2n, so it is linear. The intuition is that the partitioning work halves each round rather than staying constant per level, which is a satisfying thing to be able to derive rather than recall.

followups.q: Is there a way to guarantee O(n) in the worst case?
followups.a: Yes, the median-of-medians algorithm, which chooses a pivot guaranteed to be reasonably central by recursively finding the median of groups of five. It achieves worst-case linear time, and it is a genuine theoretical result worth naming. In practice it is rarely used because its constant factor is large enough that randomised quickselect beats it on real data, so the usual engineering answer is randomisation plus a fallback if the recursion depth degrades, mirroring introsort.

followups.q: Why clone the array, and when would you not?
followups.a: Because quickselect reorders the array as a side effect, and a method named KthSmallest that scrambles its input is a nasty surprise, exactly as with ContainsDuplicate and sorting. The clone costs O(n) time and space, which does not change the asymptotic bound but is real. If the caller does not care, or is passing a temporary, an overload that operates in place is worth offering, documented clearly. The important part is that the mutation is a deliberate, stated choice rather than an accident.

followups.q: When would you use a heap instead?
followups.a: When the data arrives as a stream, since quickselect needs the whole array materialised and revisits it repeatedly. A bounded min-heap of size k handles unbounded input in O(k) memory and gives the answer at any moment, at O(n log k) time. So quickselect wins on a static array in memory, and the heap wins for streams, for very small k relative to n, or when the input must not be touched at all.

question: Count inversions in an array.

followups.q: Why does taking one element from the right half count a whole block of inversions?
followups.a: Because both halves are already sorted at that point. If `buffer[j]` is smaller than `buffer[i]`, it is also smaller than everything after `buffer[i]` in the left half, and all of those sit at earlier positions in the original array. So every one of the `mid - i + 1` remaining left elements forms an inversion with it. Counting them individually would be the quadratic algorithm again; counting them as a block is exactly what makes it O(n log n).

followups.q: Why should the return type be long rather than int?
followups.a: Because the maximum is n(n-1)/2, which for an array of 100,000 elements is about five billion and overflows a signed 32-bit int. A reversed array of that size is not exotic. The test with [5,4,3,2,1] giving 10 is the shape of that formula at small scale. This is the same overflow reasoning as in climbing stairs and the missing-number sum: work out the maximum the answer can reach before choosing the type.

followups.q: Suppose you needed inversions within a sliding window, or after updates.
followups.a: Merge sort computes it once over a static array and cannot be updated incrementally. For dynamic data you use a Fenwick tree or an order-statistic tree: process elements left to right, and for each one query how many already-inserted values exceed it, then insert. That is O(n log n) too, but supports insertions and deletions, so it handles updates and windows. It also needs coordinate compression when values are large or sparse, which is the usual practical wrinkle.

question: Find the k closest points to the origin.

followups.q: Why compare squared distances rather than real distances?
followups.a: Because the square root is strictly increasing, so it preserves order and comparing squares gives identical rankings. Skipping it removes n square-root operations and, more importantly, keeps the arithmetic in integers, avoiding any floating-point rounding that could make two genuinely different distances compare equal. The `long` cast matters too: coordinates near int.MaxValue would overflow when squared in int. Only take the root if the caller actually needs the distance value.

followups.q: Why a max-heap for the k CLOSEST, which sounds backwards?
followups.a: Because you need cheap access to the worst member of the set you are keeping, so it can be evicted when something better arrives. The heap holds the k closest seen so far, and its root is the furthest of those. A min-heap would put the closest at the root, which you never want to remove, and you would have to hold all n points. The general rule is that a bounded top-k needs a heap ordered opposite to the direction you are selecting, which is the same reasoning as the kth-largest problem.

followups.q: Suppose the points arrive as a stream of millions, or are spread across machines.
followups.a: The heap already handles a stream in O(k) memory, which is its main advantage over quickselect. Across machines, compute the local top k on each shard and merge the results, since the global top k must be a subset of the union of the local ones. That is a genuinely useful property and makes the problem embarrassingly parallel. If instead the query were 'all points within radius r', a spatial index such as a k-d tree or an R-tree would be the right structure rather than a heap.

question: Find the median from a data stream.

followups.q: Why push every value through the low heap first instead of comparing against the roots?
followups.a: Because comparing requires handling the empty-heap case and getting the boundary right when the value equals a root, which is where hand-written versions usually break. Entering through the low heap and immediately promoting its maximum to the high heap guarantees the ordering invariant unconditionally, and the single rebalance restores the size invariant. It costs one extra heap operation per insert, a constant factor, in exchange for code with no special cases.

followups.q: Suppose you needed the median of a sliding window rather than the whole stream.
followups.a: The two-heap idea still applies but removal becomes the problem, since a heap cannot delete an arbitrary element efficiently. The standard fix is lazy deletion: keep a dictionary of values pending removal and discard them when they surface at a root, tracking the effective sizes separately. That keeps O(log n) amortised. The cleaner alternative is an order-statistic tree or an indexed skip list, which supports both arbitrary deletion and rank queries directly.

followups.q: Suppose the stream is far too large to hold in memory.
followups.a: Then an exact median is impossible without storing everything, so you move to approximation. A t-digest or the Greenwald-Khanna algorithm gives quantiles with a bounded error in a small, fixed amount of memory, and t-digest is deliberately more accurate at the tails, which is why monitoring systems use it for p99 latency. Reservoir sampling is the simpler option when a rough answer suffices. Naming the point where exactness has to be traded away is the substance of this follow-up.

followups.q: Why negate the priority rather than supply a custom comparer?
followups.a: Either works. Negation is shorter and avoids an interface dispatch per comparison, so it is marginally faster. Its flaw is int.MinValue, which has no positive counterpart and negates to itself, so a stream containing it would order incorrectly. A comparer using `Comparer<int>.Create((a, b) => b.CompareTo(a))` has no such edge case and states the intent more clearly. For production I would use the comparer and note why.

question: Reorganize a string so no two adjacent characters are the same.

followups.q: Why is (n + 1) / 2 the exact impossibility threshold?
followups.a: Because separating k copies of a character requires k - 1 gaps between them, so the string needs at least 2k - 1 positions. Rearranging, k must be at most (n + 1) / 2 with integer division. At exactly that bound the character occupies every alternate slot starting at the first, which is achievable; one more and two copies must touch. Checking it up front is worth doing because it converts a construction that would fail partway into a clean early return.

followups.q: Why hold the previous character aside rather than just excluding it in the comparison?
followups.a: Because the heap has no way to skip its root conditionally; peeking past it would mean removing and restoring, which is the same operation with more steps. Holding it outside the heap for exactly one iteration expresses the cooldown directly: it is ineligible now and eligible next time. It is the same pattern as the cooldown queue in task scheduler, and it generalises: for a cooldown of n you hold a queue of n pending items rather than a single variable.

followups.q: Suppose the required distance were k rather than 1.
followups.a: Replace the single held character with a queue of the last k used, releasing the front back into the heap once k slots have passed. If the heap empties while the queue is non-empty, the arrangement is impossible and you either pad with idle slots, as in task scheduler, or report failure, depending on the problem. That generalisation is why these two questions are often asked together: they are the same greedy with a different cooldown length and a different failure policy.

followups.q: Why does the test verify a property rather than compare against an expected string?
followups.a: Because several arrangements are valid: "aba" and, for larger inputs, many permutations all satisfy the constraint. Asserting one exact output would make the test depend on heap tie-breaking, which is unspecified and can change between runtime versions. Checking the real requirements, that no two adjacent characters match and the length is preserved, is both stronger and stable. The same argument applies to find-peak-element and to any problem with multiple correct answers.

question: Task scheduler: minimum intervals with cooldown n between same tasks.

followups.q: Why take the maximum against tasks.Length?
followups.a: Because the formula only counts the frame built by the most frequent task and assumes everything else fits inside its gaps. When there are many distinct tasks, the gaps overflow and the schedule is simply back-to-back with no idling, so the answer is the total number of tasks. Without that guard the formula would under-report. The [A,A,A,B,B,B] with n=0 case is the smallest example: the frame gives 4 but the true answer is 6.

followups.q: Why does the number of tasks tied at the maximum matter?
followups.a: Because every task occurring maxCount times must appear in the final block alongside the most frequent one, extending the schedule by one slot each. With A and B both appearing three times and n = 2, the pattern is A B idle A B idle A B, so the last block holds both, giving 8 rather than 7. Forgetting the tie count is the most common error, and it only shows up when two tasks share the top frequency.

followups.q: Suppose you had to output the actual schedule, not just its length.
followups.a: The formula gives no schedule, so you switch to simulation: a max-heap of remaining counts, popping the most frequent available task each interval and holding cooled-down tasks in a queue until they become eligible again. That is O(total log 26) and produces a concrete ordering. It is a good illustration that a closed-form count and a constructive algorithm are different things, and that being asked for the arrangement rather than the number can change the approach entirely.

question: Design a hash set / hash map from scratch.

followups.q: Why mask the hash code rather than taking the absolute value?
followups.a: Because Math.Abs(int.MinValue) throws, since its negation does not fit in an int. Masking off the sign bit with 0x7FFFFFFF maps any hash into the non-negative range with no special case and no branch. It does mean two hash codes differing only in the sign bit collide, which is harmless given they were already going to be reduced modulo the capacity. It is the same two's-complement asymmetry that bites in reverse-integer and in Pow.

followups.q: Separate chaining or open addressing?
followups.a: Chaining is simpler, degrades gracefully under a high load factor, and handles deletion cleanly. Open addressing stores entries directly in the array, which gives far better cache locality and no per-entry allocation, so it is usually faster in practice - but deletion needs tombstones and the table degrades badly as it fills. .NET's Dictionary uses chaining with entries in a flat array, which gets much of the locality benefit while keeping chaining's simplicity.

followups.q: Why does resizing need to capture next before relinking?
followups.a: Because moving an entry into the new array overwrites its Next pointer, and the old chain is traversed through that same field. Capturing the successor first is the same discipline as reversing a linked list. Losing it silently truncates every chain, so most entries disappear - which the test detects by checking all twenty keys are still present after the resize rather than just checking the count.

followups.q: What makes a hash function good, and what happens with a bad one?
followups.a: It should distribute keys uniformly and be cheap to compute. A poor one that maps many keys to the same bucket turns every operation into a linear scan of one long chain, so the map degrades to a list. That is exploitable: hash-flooding attacks deliberately collide keys to make a server's dictionary quadratic, which is why .NET randomises string hashing per process. It is worth knowing that the O(1) guarantee is an average over a good hash, not a worst case.

question: Longest substring with at most k distinct characters.

followups.q: What breaks if you leave zero-count entries in the dictionary?
followups.a: `counts.Count` would include characters no longer in the window, so the shrink loop would believe there are more distinct characters than there really are and keep contracting past the correct boundary. The answer comes out too small, and only on inputs where a character fully leaves and the window later grows again. It is a quiet failure that survives simple test cases, which is why removing at zero rather than merely decrementing is worth calling out explicitly.

followups.q: How does this relate to the longest substring without repeating characters?
followups.a: That problem is this one with k equal to the alphabet size in effect, or more precisely it is the same window with a different invariant: no character may repeat, rather than at most k distinct. Both are elastic windows differing only in the shrink condition and in what state is maintained. Seeing the whole family as one skeleton with a pluggable invariant is what makes the next variant quick to write rather than a fresh puzzle.

followups.q: Suppose k were fixed at 2 and performance mattered.
followups.a: You could replace the dictionary with two character variables and their last-seen indices, removing all hashing and allocation. That is the classic 'fruit into baskets' problem, and the specialised version is noticeably faster for a hot path. The trade-off is that it no longer generalises, so I would only specialise after measuring, and would keep the general version alongside it for clarity.

question: Find all pairs with a given difference k.

followups.q: Why is k equal to zero a genuinely different question?
followups.a: Because every value trivially satisfies value minus value equals zero, so a membership test would report every element as a pair with itself. What is actually being asked is whether the value appears at least twice, which needs counts rather than a set. Solutions that only use a HashSet return every distinct value as a pair when k is zero, which is the standard failure. It is the same self-pairing trap as the two-sum variant where the target is double a stored value.

followups.q: Why iterate the dictionary rather than the array?
followups.a: Because iterating the array would emit a pair once per occurrence of the smaller value, so an array with five 1s and one 3 would report the pair [1,3] five times. Iterating distinct values produces each pair once, which is what the problem wants. It also makes the work proportional to distinct values rather than to the array length, which matters when duplication is heavy. The trade is that you must have built the counts first, which you need anyway for the k-equals-zero case.

followups.q: How would the sorted-input version differ?
followups.a: Two pointers with no extra space: advance the fast pointer while the difference is too small and the slow one while it is too large, which is O(n) after the sort and O(1) space. If the input arrives sorted, that is strictly better. If it does not, sorting costs O(n log n), so the hash approach wins. It is the same trade as two-sum versus two-sum-on-sorted-input: a precondition in the problem statement points directly at the intended technique.

question: Count the number of set bits (Hamming weight).

followups.q: Why does n &= n - 1 clear the lowest set bit?
followups.a: Subtracting one from a binary number turns its lowest set bit into a zero and turns every bit below it into a one. ANDing that with the original keeps only the bits above the lowest set bit, since the lowest one is now zero on one side and everything below it is zero on the other. For 1100, subtracting one gives 1011, and the AND gives 1000. The same identity gives the power-of-two test, since a number with exactly one set bit becomes zero after one clearing.

followups.q: Why use uint rather than int here?
followups.a: Because right-shifting a negative int in C# performs an arithmetic shift, filling with ones, so a loop shifting until the value reaches zero would never terminate for a negative input. Using uint makes the shift logical and the loop safe. The Kernighan version above happens to work for int too, since subtraction and AND are bit patterns rather than arithmetic in this context, but declaring the parameter unsigned states the intent that the value is a bit pattern rather than a number.

followups.q: When does the difference between these actually matter?
followups.a: Rarely in application code, and a great deal in hot loops. PopCount is a single instruction on modern hardware and is what you should use in .NET 6 or later. Kernighan's is the right hand-rolled fallback and is dramatically faster on sparse values, since a number with two set bits loops twice rather than 32 times. The naive version is worth writing only to explain the problem. Population count matters in practice for bitset operations, Bloom filters, chess engines and similarity measures such as Hamming distance.

question: Single number: find the element that appears once (others twice).

followups.q: Explain the n & -n trick for isolating the lowest set bit.
followups.a: Negation in two's complement is bitwise inversion plus one, which leaves the lowest set bit unchanged while inverting everything above it. ANDing the original with its negation therefore keeps exactly that one bit. For 1100, the negation is 0100, and the AND gives 0100. It is the standard idiom for extracting the lowest set bit and is also the basis of how Fenwick trees compute their index ranges.

followups.q: What if every other element appears three times rather than twice?
followups.a: XOR no longer cancels, since three copies leave one behind.
