The usual solutions are to count set bits per position across all numbers and take each count modulo three, which leaves the bits of the lone value, or to use two accumulators tracking bits seen once and twice with a small state machine. The first is easier to explain and O(32n), the second is O(n) with a few operations. Recognising that the cancellation property is specific to pairs is the key insight.

followups.q: Why does this work for negative numbers?
followups.a: Because XOR operates on the bit pattern, not on the numeric interpretation, so two's complement representation is irrelevant to the cancellation. Any value XORed with itself is zero regardless of sign. That is a genuine advantage over sum-based approaches, which can overflow, and over approaches that assume a value range. It also means the technique extends unchanged to any fixed-width type.

question: Reverse the bits of a 32-bit integer.

followups.q: Why does using int rather than uint break this?
followups.a: Because `>>` on a signed int in C# is an arithmetic shift, propagating the sign bit, so a negative value never becomes zero by shifting and the high bits fill with ones rather than zeros. The loop would produce a corrupted result. C# does have `>>>` for an unsigned right shift since version 11, but declaring the parameter as uint is clearer: it says the value is a bit pattern, not a number, which is exactly what a bit-reversal operates on.

followups.q: How does the mask version work?
followups.a: Each step swaps groups of a given size. The 0xAAAAAAAA mask selects the odd-positioned bits and 0x55555555 the even ones, so shifting each toward the other and ORing swaps every adjacent pair. Doubling the group size each step swaps pairs, then nibbles, then bytes, then the two halves, and after five steps every bit has travelled to its mirrored position. It is the same divide-and-conquer shape as a butterfly network, and the identical structure computes a population count.

followups.q: Where does bit reversal actually matter?
followups.a: In fast Fourier transforms, where the output arrives in bit-reversed index order and must be permuted back. It also appears in some hashing and interleaving schemes, and in hardware contexts where a bus or protocol transmits bits in the opposite order to the host's convention. Outside those it is rare, which is worth saying: the question tests bit manipulation fluency more than it tests a routinely needed operation.

question: Sum of two integers without using + or -.

followups.q: Why does this work for negative numbers without any special handling?
followups.a: Because two's complement is designed so that addition is the same bit operation regardless of sign. The hardware adder does not know or care whether a bit pattern represents a negative number; the representation was chosen precisely so that one circuit handles both. That is also why subtraction is just addition of the negation, and why the negation itself is bitwise-NOT plus one, which the Subtract method uses.

followups.q: Why use uint for the intermediates?
followups.a: Because shifting the carry left can push a bit into the sign position, and in a checked arithmetic context a signed overflow would throw rather than wrap. Using uint makes the operations pure bit manipulation with defined wrapping behaviour. The cast back at the end reinterprets the bits, which is exactly what is wanted. The int.MaxValue plus one test confirms it wraps identically to ordinary addition rather than throwing.

followups.q: Is this ever useful in practice?
followups.a: Almost never directly, since the CPU has an adder. It matters conceptually in three places: understanding how hardware adders are built, since this is a ripple-carry adder in software; in constant-time cryptographic code where you sometimes avoid operations with data-dependent timing; and in certain bit-parallel algorithms that add many small values packed into one word at once. As an interview question it is testing whether you understand what addition actually is rather than testing a needed skill.

question: Find the two numbers that appear once (others twice).

followups.q: Why does partitioning on one differing bit work?
followups.a: Because two equal numbers agree on every bit, so both copies of any duplicate fall into the same group whatever bit you choose. The two singles disagree on the chosen bit by construction, so they fall into different groups. Each group therefore contains one single and some complete pairs, and XORing it cancels the pairs and leaves the single. The choice of which differing bit is arbitrary; the lowest is simply the cheapest to isolate.

followups.q: Does x & -x work for int.MinValue?
followups.a: Yes, and it is worth checking rather than assuming. int.MinValue is a single set bit in the sign position, and its two's-complement negation is itself, so the AND returns the same value. The partition still works because that bit genuinely distinguishes the two singles. The last test case includes it deliberately, since a solution using Math.Abs somewhere in the bit isolation would throw on exactly that input.

followups.q: What if three numbers appeared once?
followups.a: The technique does not extend directly, because the XOR of three values gives no clean partition - a bit where all three differ does not exist in general, and splitting on one bit can leave two singles in the same group. The standard approach is more involved, using the fact that at least one group must contain exactly one single and recursing, or counting set bits per position modulo the repetition factor. The two-single case is special precisely because one differing bit is enough.

question: Counting bits: number of set bits for every number 0..n.

followups.q: Why is i & (i - 1) guaranteed to be a smaller, already-computed index?
followups.a: Because clearing the lowest set bit strictly decreases the value, so the index is always below i and was filled on an earlier iteration. That ordering is what makes a single forward loop valid with no recursion or memo checks. It is also why the recurrence is exactly 'one fewer set bit': the operation removes precisely one bit, so the count is one more than that of the result.

followups.q: Which of the two formulations do you prefer?
followups.a: The shift version is usually easier for a reader to verify, since 'drop the last bit and add it back' is immediately intuitive, whereas the AND version requires knowing the clearing identity. They are the same complexity and performance. I would write the shift version with a brief comment, and mention the AND version as the variant that generalises to problems where you want to iterate over set bits rather than over all bits.

followups.q: Could you just call PopCount in a loop?
followups.a: Yes, and with hardware popcount it is a single instruction per number, so in practice it is competitive and arguably simpler. The DP is O(n) against O(n) with a larger constant for a software popcount, or O(n) either way with hardware support. The DP's real advantage is that it needs no intrinsic and is portable, and that it demonstrates the recurrence, which is what the question is testing. For production on .NET 6 or later I would use BitOperations.PopCount.

question: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put.

followups.q: How would you make this thread-safe, and what does that cost?
followups.a: The simplest correct answer is a single lock around both operations, because even `Get` mutates the recency list, so a reader-writer lock buys nothing. That serialises the cache and makes it a contention point under load. The realistic alternatives are sharding into N independent caches keyed by hash of the key, which cuts contention by roughly N, or switching to an approximate policy such as CLRU or a TinyLFU-style sketch where reads only set a bit and reordering happens in batches off the hot path. Production caches almost always pick approximate recency over exact recency for precisely this reason.

followups.q: What if entries also need a time-to-live?
followups.a: Store an expiry timestamp in the node value and treat an expired entry as a miss on read, evicting it lazily at that point. Lazy expiry alone lets dead entries occupy capacity, so pair it with either a periodic sweep or a second structure ordered by expiry, such as a min-heap or a timer wheel, to reclaim proactively. Note that TTL eviction and LRU eviction are independent policies and both must be able to remove a node, which is another reason for the doubly linked list.

followups.q: Why not just use MemoryCache or ConcurrentDictionary?
followups.a: In production you generally should: `MemoryCache` already implements size limits, TTL, and eviction callbacks, and is thread-safe. `ConcurrentDictionary` on its own is not a cache, because it has no eviction policy and will grow without bound. The hand-rolled version matters when you need a strict bound with predictable O(1) behaviour and no background scanning, or when you are being asked the question to demonstrate the data-structure reasoning.

followups.q: Your capacity check uses the dictionary count. Is there a case where that is wrong?
followups.a: It is correct here only because the map and the list are always mutated together, and the update path removes before it inserts. If a later change added an entry to one structure without the other, or allowed the same key to be present twice in the list, the count would drift from the true size. That invariant, that every dictionary value is a node currently in the list and vice versa, is the thing worth stating explicitly in review.

question: Design an LFU cache.

followups.q: Why can minFrequency be maintained in O(1) rather than searched for?
followups.a: Because it only changes in two ways. Inserting a new item sets it to 1, since nothing can be less frequent. Promoting an item raises its frequency by exactly one, so if that emptied the minimum list, the new minimum must be exactly one higher; nothing else could have become the minimum in between. Those two rules cover every mutation, so no search over the frequency keys is ever needed. Without that observation you would scan for the minimum and lose the O(1) guarantee.

followups.q: How does LFU compare with LRU in practice?
followups.a: LFU resists scans better: a one-off sweep through many keys does not evict the genuinely popular items, whereas it flushes an LRU cache entirely. Its weakness is the mirror image, cache pollution: an item that was very popular last week keeps a high count and refuses to leave even though it is now dead. Real caches therefore use aged or windowed variants such as TinyLFU, which decays counts over time, or W-TinyLFU as used by Caffeine, which combines a small LRU window with a frequency sketch.

followups.q: Suppose the interviewer says this uses too much memory for millions of keys.
followups.a: The per-entry overhead is the problem: two dictionary entries plus a linked-list node per key. The standard answer is to stop tracking exact frequencies and use a Count-Min Sketch, which estimates counts in a fixed amount of memory with a bounded error and never underestimates. Combined with a small admission window that keeps new items alive long enough to prove themselves, that is exactly the TinyLFU design, and it gives near-optimal hit rates at a fraction of the memory.

followups.q: How would you make this thread-safe?
followups.a: A single lock around both operations, because even Get mutates three structures and a reader would otherwise observe a node mid-move between frequency lists. A reader-writer lock buys nothing since every path writes. That makes the cache a contention point, so the realistic fixes are sharding by key hash, which cuts contention roughly by the shard count, or moving to an approximate policy where reads only touch a sketch and reordering happens in batches off the hot path.

question: Design a rate limiter (token bucket).

followups.q: What does capacity actually control versus the refill rate?
followups.a: The refill rate sets the sustained throughput, the long-run requests per second a client is allowed. Capacity sets the burst: the largest number of requests that can be served back to back after an idle period. They are tuned separately, and conflating them is the usual bug. A capacity equal to one token gives a strict, evenly spaced limiter with no burst tolerance, which is effectively the leaky-bucket behaviour.

followups.q: How does this change when there are many API instances behind a load balancer?
followups.a: Per-instance buckets mean the effective limit is the configured rate multiplied by the instance count, and it shifts every time you scale. The state has to move to something shared, usually Redis, with the read-modify-write performed atomically in a Lua script or via `INCR` on a fixed window. That adds a network round trip to every request and makes the limiter a dependency of availability, so the common compromise is a local bucket sized to the instance's share, refreshed periodically from a central allocator, accepting slightly fuzzy enforcement in exchange for no hot-path dependency.

followups.q: Token bucket versus sliding window: when would you pick the other one?
followups.a: Sliding window counts actual requests within a moving time range, so it enforces a hard ceiling with no burst beyond the configured count. Token bucket is smoother and cheaper, but permits a burst up to capacity. Pick sliding window when the limit is contractual, such as a billing quota where 101 requests in a minute genuinely must fail. Pick token bucket when you are protecting a resource and short bursts are harmless. Fixed window is cheapest but suffers the boundary problem, where 2x the limit passes across the seam of two adjacent windows.

followups.q: What should the server return when a request is rejected?
followups.a: HTTP 429 with a `Retry-After` header, and ideally `RateLimit-Limit`, `RateLimit-Remaining` and `RateLimit-Reset` so a well-behaved client can pace itself instead of retrying blindly. Computing `Retry-After` from the bucket is straightforward: it is the shortfall in tokens divided by the refill rate. In .NET 7+ this is what the built-in `RateLimiter` middleware gives you, with `TokenBucketRateLimiter` as one of its policies.

question: Insert Delete GetRandom in O(1).

followups.q: What exactly breaks if you forget to update the moved element's index?
followups.a: The dictionary keeps pointing the moved value at its old, now-invalid position. A later Remove of that value would overwrite the wrong slot, corrupting the list and losing a different element, and GetRandom could return a value no longer in the set. It is a silent corruption rather than an exception, which makes it the worst kind of bug. The test removing a non-last element exists specifically to exercise that path.

followups.q: Why not just use a HashSet and pick a random element from it?
followups.a: Because a HashSet has no indexing, so selecting a uniformly random member means enumerating to a random position, which is O(n). The whole design exists to give random access, and the list provides that while the dictionary provides membership. It is a good example of combining two structures so that each covers the other's weakness, which is the same idea as the LRU cache pairing a dictionary with a linked list.

followups.q: How would you support duplicates?
followups.a: Change the dictionary to map each value to a HashSet of indices rather than a single one. Remove takes any index from that set, and the swap updates the moved value's index set by removing the old position and adding the new one. GetRandom is unchanged and naturally becomes weighted by multiplicity, which is usually what is wanted. The fiddly case is when the element being removed is itself the last one, where the swap is a no-op and the order of the set updates matters.

followups.q: Why does the test assert membership rather than a specific random value?
followups.a: Because the output of a seeded Random is an implementation detail that is not guaranteed stable across .NET versions, so asserting an exact draw would make the test fragile for reasons unrelated to the code. Checking that the drawn value is a current member tests the actual contract. The same reasoning applies to Fisher-Yates and to any problem where several answers are correct.

question: Design a data structure for autocomplete / typeahead.

followups.q: Why cache the top k at every node rather than collecting on demand?
followups.a: Because a short prefix can have an enormous subtree: typing 'a' on a real search engine matches millions of phrases, and traversing them per keystroke is hopeless. Caching moves the work to write time, where it happens far less often, and makes the read O(prefix length) regardless of how popular the prefix is. The cost is memory, k entries per node, and slower writes. For a read-dominated workload like typeahead that is exactly the right direction.

followups.q: The Add path re-sorts a list at every node. Is that acceptable?
followups.a: It is O(prefix length x k log k), which is fine for k of three or ten but sloppy. A production version would keep each node's list as a small bounded heap or do an insertion into an already-sorted list, which is O(k) rather than O(k log k). The bigger real-world change is to rebuild the caches offline in batch rather than updating synchronously on every write, since suggestion freshness rarely needs to be immediate.

followups.q: Suppose suggestions must be personalised per user.
followups.a: A single shared trie no longer suffices, since ranking differs per user. The usual architecture is a shared global trie for candidate generation, returning a few dozen prefix matches cheaply, followed by a per-user ranking pass that blends global popularity with personal history. That separation of candidate generation from ranking is the standard shape of every recommendation system, and it keeps the expensive personalised work proportional to the candidate count rather than the corpus.

followups.q: How would you handle typos, so 'recieve' still suggests 'receive'?
followups.a: Exact prefix matching cannot, so you add fuzzy matching: either a BK-tree or a Levenshtein automaton, which walks the trie allowing a bounded edit distance, or a precomputed set of common misspellings. Walking the trie with an edit budget is the elegant option because it reuses the structure you already have, and pruning branches whose best possible distance already exceeds the budget keeps it tractable.

question: Implement a min stack / max stack with O(1) extremum.

followups.q: Why does the comparison need to be <= rather than <?
followups.a: Because equal values must each be recorded. With two 2s pushed and a strict less-than, only the first would go onto the minima stack; popping the second 2 would then match the top and pop the record, leaving the stack reporting a minimum of 5 while a 2 is still present. The test does exactly this. The mirror argument applies to the maxima stack with >=. It is one character and it decides correctness.

followups.q: Can this be done in O(1) extra space?
followups.a: There is a well-known encoding trick: when a new minimum arrives, push `2 * value - currentMin`, a value provably below the new minimum, and decode the previous minimum on pop. It achieves O(1) extra space but risks overflow for values near the type's limits and is genuinely hard to read. I would not ship it. The conditional-push version above is already O(1) amortised for typical data and stays obvious, which is the better trade outside a puzzle.

followups.q: How does this relate to the sliding window maximum problem?
followups.a: Both maintain an extremum under changing contents, but the access patterns differ. A stack only ever adds and removes at one end, so a parallel stack suffices. A window adds at one end and removes at the other, which a stack cannot express, so it needs a monotonic deque instead. Recognising that the structure follows from where mutations happen, rather than from what is being computed, is the transferable point.

question: Design Twitter (post tweet, get news feed, follow/unfollow).

followups.q: Why a counter rather than DateTime for the timestamp?
followups.a: Because two tweets posted in the same tick would tie, and the ordering between them would then depend on unspecified sort stability. A monotonic counter guarantees a strict total order with no ties. It also avoids clock adjustments moving tweets around, which is the same reason Stopwatch is preferred over DateTime.UtcNow for measuring elapsed time. In a distributed system this becomes a logical clock or a Snowflake-style id embedding both time and a sequence number.

followups.q: This is pull-on-read. When would you push on write instead?
followups.a: Fan-out on write precomputes each follower's feed when a tweet is posted, making reads a single lookup. That suits the common case where reads vastly outnumber writes. It collapses for celebrities: a user with fifty million followers would trigger fifty million writes per tweet. Real systems use a hybrid, fanning out for ordinary users and merging on read for the few accounts with huge followings, which is exactly the design Twitter published.

followups.q: Why pull each user's next tweet lazily rather than loading all of them?
followups.a: Because the feed needs only ten entries, so loading every tweet from every followee would be enormously wasteful for an active user following hundreds of accounts. The heap holds at most one entry per source and pulls the next only when one is consumed, so the total work is proportional to the feed size and the number of sources rather than to the total tweet count. It is the same merge-k-sorted-lists technique, and the laziness is what makes it practical.

followups.q: What breaks first if this were real?
followups.a: Memory, since everything is in process and nothing is evicted or persisted. Then the follow set for celebrity accounts, which would be millions of entries in a single HashSet. Then the lack of any pagination, since GetNewsFeed only ever returns the newest ten with no cursor to continue from. In a real design the tweets live in a partitioned store keyed by user and time, feeds are cached in Redis, and the API is cursor-based so clients can page backwards.

question: FizzBuzz.

followups.q: How would you make the rules configurable, so a third rule can be added without touching the loop?
followups.a: Pass the rules in as data, for example a list of `(int divisor, string word)` ordered by divisor, and have the loop append every word whose divisor divides the number. Adding 'Bang' for 7 is then a one-line data change with no new branches, and the combined cases such as 21 and 105 fall out automatically. That is the actual point of the question in most interviews: not whether you can write it, but whether your first instinct is a chain of if-else that doubles with every new rule.

followups.q: Would you return a collection instead of printing?
followups.a: Yes, for anything but a toy. A method that writes to the console is untestable without capturing standard output and unusable from anywhere that is not a console. Returning `IEnumerable<string>`, ideally with `yield return` so it streams and does not materialise n strings at once, separates the computation from the presentation and makes it trivially unit-testable. The console write then lives in `Main`, which is where I/O belongs.

followups.q: Is the modulo worth avoiding for performance?
followups.a: You can replace it with two counters that increment and reset at 3 and 5, avoiding the division entirely, and on very large ranges that is measurably faster. But it is almost always the wrong trade: the code gets harder to read for a saving that is invisible next to the cost of writing the output. The honest answer is to say you would keep the modulo, and that if this genuinely were the bottleneck the fix would be to stop doing per-line console writes, which dominate everything else here by orders of magnitude.

question: Count primes up to n (Sieve of Eratosthenes).

followups.q: Why start crossing off at p squared rather than 2p?
followups.a: Because every multiple of p below p squared has a prime factor smaller than p and was therefore already crossed off when that smaller prime was processed. For p equal to 7, the multiples 14, 21, 28 and 35 were handled by 2, 3, 2 and 5 respectively, so the first new one is 49. It is a genuine saving, not just a tidiness point: it removes a large fraction of the redundant writes and is one of the two reasons the sieve is near-linear.

followups.q: Why does the outer loop stop at the square root?
followups.a: Because if a number below n is composite, it has at least one factor at or below its own square root, hence at or below the square root of n. So every composite has already been marked by the time p exceeds that bound, and continuing would only re-examine primes with nothing left to cross off. The `(long)p * p` cast matters here: for n near int.MaxValue, computing p squared in int overflows and the loop condition misbehaves.

followups.q: What if n were far too large for an array of n booleans?
followups.a: A bool per number wastes eight bits each, so the first step is a bitset, cutting memory eightfold, and skipping even numbers halves it again. Beyond that you use a segmented sieve: sieve the small primes up to the square root once, then process the range in cache-sized blocks, which keeps memory bounded and improves locality dramatically. That is how primes are counted into the billions, and it is the expected answer once the naive array stops fitting.

question: Pow(x, n): implement fast exponentiation.

followups.q: Why widen the exponent to long before negating it?
followups.a: Because int.MinValue is -2147483648 and int.MaxValue is 2147483647, so its negation does not fit in an int and wraps back to itself. The loop would then never terminate or would compute the wrong answer. Widening to long before negating gives room for the positive value. It is the classic asymmetry of two's complement, and this problem is where it most often bites, which is why MyPow(1, int.MinValue) is in the tests.

followups.q: Why is this the standard algorithm in cryptography?
followups.a: Because RSA and Diffie-Hellman raise numbers to enormous exponents modulo a large prime, and a linear loop would take longer than the age of the universe. Exponentiation by squaring turns a 2048-bit exponent into about 2048 modular multiplications. Real implementations also need it to run in constant time regardless of the exponent's bits, since the branch on odd exponents leaks information through timing, which is a genuine side-channel attack.

followups.q: Why iterative rather than recursive?
followups.a: The recursive version is arguably clearer, halving the exponent and squaring the result, and its depth is only log n so there is no stack risk. The iterative version avoids call overhead and makes the accumulation explicit, which matters in the modular variant where it is a hot path. Either is defensible here; I would write the recursive one in an interview for clarity and the iterative one in a library.

question: Greatest common divisor (Euclidean algorithm).

followups.q: Why divide before multiplying in the LCM?
followups.a: Because `a * b` can overflow even when the LCM itself fits comfortably. The last test multiplies two values near a billion, whose product is around 10^18 and only just fits in a long, and slightly larger inputs would wrap silently. Dividing first keeps the intermediate close to the final answer. The division is always exact, since the gcd divides a by definition, so nothing is lost by reordering.

followups.q: What is the worst case for the Euclidean algorithm?
followups.a: Consecutive Fibonacci numbers, which produce the maximum number of steps for their size, because each remainder step drops to the previous Fibonacci number rather than falling faster. That is Lamé's theorem, and it is the origin of the O(log min(a,b)) bound. It is a nice result to know because it shows the algorithm is not merely fast in practice but has a proven bound driven by a recognisable family of inputs.

followups.q: What is the extended Euclidean algorithm for?
followups.a: It computes not just the gcd but also coefficients x and y such that ax + by equals the gcd. That is how you find a modular multiplicative inverse, which underpins RSA key generation and the Chinese Remainder Theorem. The standard gcd tells you whether an inverse exists, since it exists exactly when the gcd is one; the extended version tells you what it is. That is the usual follow-up once the basic algorithm is written.

question: Reverse an integer with overflow handling.

followups.q: Why are the boundary digits 7 and -8?
followups.a: Because int.MaxValue is 2147483647 and int.MinValue is -2147483648, so their last digits are 7 and 8. When the accumulated value equals MaxValue / 10, which is 214748364, appending any digit above 7 overflows. The negative side mirrors it with -8. Those magic numbers come straight from the type's limits, and deriving them rather than recalling them is what makes the check convincing in an interview.

followups.q: Why does the negative case need no special handling in the digit extraction?
followups.a: Because C#'s modulo keeps the sign of the dividend, so -123 % 10 is -3 rather than 7, and the accumulated result stays negative throughout. That means one loop handles both signs. In Python the modulo floors instead and would give 7, so the same code there needs an explicit sign extraction. It is a genuine portability trap when translating numeric code between the two languages.

followups.q: Could you use a long or checked arithmetic instead?
followups.a: Accumulating in a long and comparing against int range at the end is simpler and perfectly correct for 32-bit input, and I would probably write that in production. The problem usually forbids it to force the boundary reasoning. `checked` arithmetic is another option, throwing on overflow and catching it to return 0, though using exceptions for expected control flow is expensive if it happens often. The manual check is the fastest and the one the question is really asking for.

question: Excel column number to title and vice versa (base-26).

followups.q: Why is this not ordinary base 26?
followups.a: Because there is no zero digit. In ordinary base 26 the digits would be 0 to 25 and the sequence after Z would be BA, since A would act as zero and AA would equal A. Excel uses bijective base 26 with digits 1 to 26, so every string maps to exactly one number and vice versa with no leading-zero ambiguity. The decrement before the modulo is what converts between the two conventions, and it is the entire difficulty of the problem.

followups.q: Using Insert(0, ...) in a loop is quadratic. Does it matter?
followups.a: Not here, because column titles are at most a few characters: Excel's limit is XFD, three letters. For a general base conversion with long outputs it would matter, and you would append and reverse once at the end, as in the add-binary problem. It is worth noticing the pattern even when the bound makes it harmless, because the same habit applied to a long string is a real performance bug.

followups.q: Where else does bijective numbering appear?
followups.a: Anywhere identifiers must be unambiguous with no leading-zero problem: spreadsheet columns, some URL shorteners, and certain invoice or ticket numbering schemes. It also appears in bijective base-k representations used in combinatorics. The general lesson is that 'looks like base k' is worth checking carefully, since the off-by-one between 0-indexed and 1-indexed digit sets is exactly the kind of thing that produces a system working for the first 25 cases and failing on the 26th.

question: Happy number: does repeatedly summing squares of digits reach 1?

followups.q: Why is this the same problem as detecting a cycle in a linked list?
followups.a: Because both follow an iterated function `x = f(x)` and ask whether the path repeats. In a list, f is 'the next node'; here it is 'the sum of squared digits'. Floyd's algorithm cares only that f is deterministic and the state space finite, not what f means. Recognising that framing is the point of the question, and it is why an interviewer often asks linked-list cycle detection first and this immediately after.

followups.q: Why is the process guaranteed to terminate?
followups.a: Because the digit-square sum shrinks large numbers rapidly and then traps them. Any number below 1000 maps to at most 3 times 81, which is 243, so once the sequence drops below 1000 it stays below 250 forever. A finite state space with a deterministic step must eventually repeat, so it either reaches 1 or enters a cycle. That bound is what guarantees the loop ends rather than running indefinitely.

followups.q: Is there a shortcut?
followups.a: Yes, and it is a curiosity worth knowing: every unhappy number eventually reaches 4, so you can simply iterate until the value is 1 or 4 and answer accordingly. It relies on an empirical fact about this specific function rather than on a general principle, so it is brittle if the rules change, for instance to cubes of digits. I would mention it as a trick but implement the cycle detection, because the latter generalises and the former does not.

question: Design a URL shortener (encode/decode).

followups.q: Counter or hash for key generation?
followups.a: A counter never collides, produces the shortest keys, and is trivially fast, but it makes ids guessable and enumerable, which leaks how many URLs exist and lets anyone walk the whole corpus. Hashing avoids that but must handle collisions, usually by probing with a salt until a free key is found. The common compromise is a counter passed through a reversible obfuscation such as Feistel or multiplication by a modular inverse, which keeps uniqueness while making the sequence unguessable.

followups.q: How would this work across multiple servers?
followups.a: A single in-process counter does not survive multiple instances. The usual options are a ticket server or database sequence handing out ranges, so each instance takes a block of a thousand ids and issues them locally without coordination; a Snowflake-style id combining a machine identifier with a timestamp and sequence; or a hash-based scheme, which needs no coordination at all but reintroduces collision handling. The range-allocation approach is usually the pragmatic winner.

followups.q: Why base 62 rather than base 64?
followups.a: Because base 64 includes characters such as plus, slash and equals that require URL encoding, which defeats the purpose of a short link. Base 62 uses only alphanumerics, which are safe in a URL path unencoded. Some services go further and exclude visually ambiguous characters such as 0, O, l and I so that links can be read aloud or copied from print without error, trading a slightly longer key for fewer support tickets.

followups.q: What would you add before calling this production-ready?
followups.a: Persistence, since an in-memory dictionary loses everything on restart. Expiry, so dead links are reclaimed. Rate limiting on the encode endpoint, or it becomes a free open redirector for spam. Validation and a blocklist on the target URL for the same reason, since open redirectors are used in phishing. And analytics on decode, which is usually the actual product. The data structures here are the easy part; the abuse surface is what makes it a real system.

question: Design a hit counter (hits in the last 5 minutes).

followups.q: Why is the stale-slot check necessary?
followups.a: Because the buffer wraps, so slot 5 is reused by second 5, second 305, second 605 and so on. Without comparing the stored timestamp, a hit at second 305 would add to the count left over from second 5, inflating the total with data that should have expired. Comparing and resetting is what makes the fixed-size buffer behave like an expiring window. It is the same idea as a generation counter used to invalidate stale entries without clearing them.

followups.q: GetHits is O(300). Could it be O(1)?
followups.a: You could maintain a running total, adjusting it as slots expire, but expiry is driven by the passage of time rather than by an event, so you would still need to sweep the slots that have gone stale since the last query. In practice 300 iterations over two small arrays is a few microseconds and entirely fine. If the window were far larger, say a day at second resolution, you would switch to hierarchical buckets: seconds rolled up into minutes and minutes into hours.

followups.q: What if hits arrive out of order, or from several threads?
followups.a: Out-of-order timestamps break the stale check, since an older hit would reset a newer slot and lose counts. The fix is to ignore hits older than the current window, which is what a real metrics pipeline does. For concurrency, the increments need to be atomic and the timestamp check and reset need to happen together, so either a lock per slot or an interlocked compare-and-swap on a packed timestamp-and-count value. Sharding the counter per thread and summing on read is the usual high-throughput answer.

followups.q: How does this relate to rate limiting?
followups.a: It is the same counting machinery with a different purpose: a fixed-window or sliding-window rate limiter asks whether the count in the recent window exceeds a threshold. The bucket-per-second approach here is effectively a sliding window log compressed into counters, which avoids the fixed-window boundary problem where twice the limit can pass across the seam of two adjacent windows. Recognising that a hit counter and a rate limiter share an implementation is a good observation to offer.

question: Longest repeating character replacement: longest substring of one repeated letter after at most k replacements.

followups.q: Why is it safe to never decrease maxCount?
followups.a: Because the answer only ever asks for the longest window, not for the window at each position to be exactly valid. If maxCount is stale and too high, the validity test is too permissive and the window is allowed to stay wider than it should, but it cannot grow, since growth requires the test to pass with the current length. So the recorded best can never exceed a genuinely achievable length. The window effectively slides at fixed width until a real improvement appears. It is correct but genuinely subtle, and it is worth saying you would add a comment in production because the next reader will assume it is a bug.

followups.q: What would recomputing maxCount properly cost?
followups.a: Scanning the 26 counts on every shrink, so O(26n) instead of O(n). That is still linear in practice and arguably clearer. If the alphabet were large or unbounded, recomputation would become genuinely expensive and you would need a max-heap or a count-of-counts structure. So the stale-maximum trick buys a constant factor and costs readability, which is a reasonable trade to decline if the team values obviousness.

followups.q: Suppose the window had to contain at most two distinct characters instead.
followups.a: That is a different sliding window: shrink while the count of distinct characters in the window exceeds two, maintained with a dictionary and a distinct counter. Both are elastic windows, but the invariant differs, which changes the shrink condition entirely. Recognising that most of these problems share one skeleton and differ only in the invariant and how cheaply it can be maintained is the transferable insight across the whole family.

question: Permutation in string: does s2 contain a permutation of s1?

followups.q: Why does the last test case return false when all the letters are present?
followups.a: Because a permutation must be contiguous and must match the multiset exactly. "hello" needs two l's and one o adjacent to an h and an e, and no window of length five in that text satisfies it. Candidates who solve this with a set of characters rather than counts, or who forget contiguity, pass the first few cases and fail this one. It is the reason the test is worth including rather than stopping at the obvious examples.

followups.q: How does this differ from finding all anagrams of a pattern?
followups.a: Only in the output: this returns a boolean and can stop at the first match, while the anagram problem collects every starting index and must scan the whole text. The window machinery is identical. That is worth saying explicitly in an interview, because recognising that two differently worded problems share an implementation is exactly what lets you write the second one quickly after the first.

followups.q: Suppose the pattern could be very long relative to the text.
followups.a: The early length check handles the impossible case, and beyond that the algorithm is already optimal at O(n) regardless of the pattern length, since the window comparison is O(1). The cost that does scale with the pattern is the initial count, which is O(m), so the total is O(n + m) and there is nothing to improve. If instead there were many patterns to test against one text, you would group them by length and by count signature so a single pass could check all patterns of the same length at once.

question: Valid palindrome II: can the string be a palindrome after deleting at most one character?

followups.q: Why must both deletion branches be tried?
followups.a: Because at a mismatch there is no local information telling you which side is the culprit. In "deeee" the mismatch is d against e, and deleting the left character works while deleting the right does not; a symmetric example exists where the opposite holds. Any heuristic that inspects only the next character can be defeated by a longer string. Testing both is O(n) in total anyway, so there is no cost to correctness here.

followups.q: How would you generalise to at most k deletions?
followups.a: The two-branch recursion becomes exponential in k, so you switch to dynamic programming: the minimum deletions to make a string a palindrome is its length minus the longest palindromic subsequence, which is O(n^2). Then compare that against k. The jump from k = 1 to general k is a jump from a linear scan to a quadratic DP, which is worth stating because it explains why the problem is posed with exactly one deletion.

followups.q: Why is the helper a plain palindrome check with no deletion budget?
followups.a: Because the single allowed deletion has already been spent at the point the helper is called, so anything further must match exactly. Passing a remaining budget would be the general-k formulation and is unnecessary here. Keeping the helper simple also makes the complexity obvious: the outer scan and the two helper calls each touch each character at most once, so the whole thing is linear rather than quadratic.

question: Isomorphic strings: can characters of s be mapped one-to-one to characters of t preserving order?

followups.q: Why is one map insufficient?
followups.a: Because it only enforces that each source character maps consistently, not that distinct sources map to distinct targets. With "ab" and "xx", a maps to x and then b maps to x, which the forward map accepts since b had no prior mapping. That is a function but not a bijection, and isomorphism requires a bijection. The reverse map catches it because x is already claimed by a. It is the test case that separates a correct solution from a plausible one.

followups.q: Could you solve it without maps at all?
followups.a: Yes, by comparing the pattern of first occurrences: transform each string into the sequence of indices where each character first appeared, and check the two sequences are identical. "egg" becomes 0,1,1 and "add" becomes 0,1,1. That uses two arrays of last-seen positions rather than dictionaries and is a neat reformulation. It also makes the relationship to the word-pattern problem explicit, since that is the same check with words instead of characters.

followups.q: How does the word pattern problem differ?
followups.a: It maps characters of a pattern to whole words rather than to characters, so the tokenisation changes but the bijection requirement is identical: you still need both directions, and the classic failure is 'abba' against 'dog dog dog dog', which one-directional checking accepts. The other trap there is comparing lengths after splitting rather than before, since a pattern of length four and three words must be rejected before the loop starts.

question: Word pattern: does a string of words follow a pattern like 'abba'?

followups.q: Why is the length check before the loop rather than inside it?
followups.a: Because indexing `words[i]` with a pattern longer than the word list throws, and a pattern shorter than the list would silently ignore the trailing words and return true for a non-match. Checking first makes both cases a clean rejection. It is the same discipline as comparing string lengths before an anagram check: cheap up front, and it removes a whole class of index errors from the main loop.

followups.q: How does RemoveEmptyEntries change the behaviour?
followups.a: It collapses runs of spaces, so "dog  cat" with two spaces parses as two words rather than three with an empty one in the middle. That is usually what you want, but it means the function silently accepts sloppy input rather than rejecting it. If the contract required exactly single-space separation, you would split without the option and validate, because quietly normalising input is sometimes hiding a caller's bug.

followups.q: This is the same shape as isomorphic strings. What is actually different?
followups.a: Only the tokenisation: characters map to words instead of to characters. The bijection requirement, the two maps and the failure mode are identical. A shared generic helper taking two sequences would serve both, which is worth saying because interviewers often ask them consecutively to see whether you recognise the repeat or start from scratch.

question: String compression: compress a character array in place as counts of repeated characters.

followups.q: Why can the write pointer never overtake the read pointer?
followups.a: Because a run of length one writes exactly one character and consumes one, and any longer run writes the character plus at most as many digits as would fit, which is always fewer than the run consumed. A run of 12 consumes 12 cells and writes 3. So the write index is always at most the read index, and no unread data can be clobbered. Stating that invariant is the substance of the question, since it is what makes the in-place requirement achievable at all.

followups.q: Why write the count digit by digit rather than as a single character?
followups.a: Because a count of 12 is two characters. Writing `(char)(count + '0')` works only for counts up to nine and silently produces a wrong character beyond that, so a run of twelve would compress to something unreadable rather than 'a12'. The twelve-character test exists precisely to catch that, and it is the single most common bug in this problem.

followups.q: The output can be longer than the input, as with 'abc'. Is that a problem?
followups.a: For this problem no, because single characters are written without a count, so the output is never longer than the input; 'abc' compresses to itself at the same length. Real run-length encoding without that rule can expand data, which is why practical compressors use a marker byte or fall back to storing a raw block when encoding would grow it. It is worth mentioning, since 'compression that sometimes makes things bigger' is a genuine property of RLE that the special case here quietly avoids.

question: Zigzag conversion: write a string in a zigzag on n rows and read it row by row.

followups.q: Why must numRows of one be special-cased?
followups.a: Because with a single row there is no bottom edge distinct from the top, so the direction never flips and the row index walks off the end of the array on the second character. The zigzag also degenerates to the original string, so returning it directly is both the correct answer and the safe one. It is the classic forgotten edge case here, and it fails with an index exception rather than a wrong answer, which at least makes it obvious once tested.

followups.q: There is a closed-form way to compute each character's row. Would you use it?
followups.a: You can: the pattern repeats every 2 * (numRows - 1) characters, so a character's row is derivable from its index modulo that cycle, with a reflection for the second half. It avoids the per-row buffers and allows reading directly in output order. It is genuinely harder to get right, especially the reflection, and saves memory rather than time. I would write the simulation first for clarity and only switch if the buffers mattered.

followups.q: Why check numRows >= s.Length separately?
followups.a: It is an optimisation rather than a correctness fix: with more rows than characters the walk never reaches the bottom, so each character lands on its own row and concatenating them returns the original string. The simulation would produce the same answer, just with wasted allocation of empty buffers. Returning early makes the intent explicit and avoids allocating potentially many unused StringBuilders when numRows is large.

question: Multiply two non-negative numbers given as strings without converting to integers.

followups.q: Why do the digits at i and j land at positions i+j and i+j+1?
followups.a: Because with left-to-right indexing, the digit at index i of an m-digit number has place value 10^(m-1-i). Multiplying two such digits gives place value 10^(m+n-2-i-j), which in an array of length m+n is index i+j+1 for the units and i+j for the carry. Deriving it rather than recalling it is worth doing, because getting the offset wrong by one shifts the entire answer by a factor of ten and the bug looks like a carry error.

followups.q: Why does the carry never overflow an int?
followups.a: Because the product of two digits is at most 81, and adding the existing slot value keeps the sum under about 100, so the carry is at most 9 or so and the accumulated value in any slot stays small. Folding the carry in immediately rather than deferring it is what keeps the bound tight; a version that summed all partial products first before carrying would accumulate much larger values and could overflow for long inputs.

followups.q: Is there a faster algorithm?
followups.a: Yes. Karatsuba multiplication splits each number in half and uses three recursive multiplications instead of four, giving roughly O(n^1.585), and it beats long multiplication once numbers reach a few hundred digits. Beyond that, FFT-based methods reach O(n log n) and are what real big-number libraries use for very large values. For interview-sized inputs the quadratic version is correct and expected, but naming Karatsuba shows you know where the ceiling is.

question: Add binary: add two binary strings and return the sum as a string.

followups.q: Why build the string backwards and reverse, rather than inserting at the front?
followups.a: Because `StringBuilder.Insert(0, ...)` shifts the entire buffer on every call, making the whole loop quadratic. Appending is amortised O(1) and a single reverse at the end is O(n), so the total stays linear. It is the same reasoning as using a StringBuilder rather than string concatenation in a loop, and it is one of the most common accidental quadratic patterns in real code.

followups.q: Why not parse to integers, add, and convert back?
followups.a: Because the inputs can exceed any built-in type. A 64-bit long caps out around 19 decimal digits or 63 binary ones, and these problems deliberately allow longer strings. `Convert.ToInt64(s, 2)` would throw or silently overflow. This is the same reason the add-two-numbers linked list and the string multiplication problems exist: they are miniature big-number arithmetic, and the string representation is the point rather than an obstacle.

followups.q: How would this change for an arbitrary base?
followups.a: Replace the modulo and division by two with the base, and map digits to characters via a lookup for bases above ten. The loop structure is unchanged. The one new concern is validating that every input character is a legal digit for the base, since an out-of-range character would silently produce a wrong result through the arithmetic rather than failing. Generalising it that way is a natural follow-up and shows the algorithm was understood rather than pattern-matched.

question: Convert an integer to a Roman numeral and a Roman numeral to an integer.

followups.q: Why include 900, 400, 90, 40, 9 and 4 in the table rather than handling subtraction separately?
followups.a: Because it turns a rule-laden conversion into a plain greedy loop. Without them, 900 would render as DCCCC and you would need post-processing rules to rewrite it as CM. Treating the subtractive pairs as first-class values means the greedy is provably correct: at each step the largest fitting value is always part of the canonical form. It is a good example of choosing a representation that makes the algorithm trivial rather than writing a clever algorithm for an awkward representation.

followups.q: Why is 3999 the upper limit?
followups.a: Because the standard symbol set stops at M for 1000, and canonical notation allows at most three consecutive identical symbols, so MMM for 3000 plus CMXCIX for 999 is the maximum. Larger numbers historically used overbars to multiply by a thousand, which has no place in the ASCII representation. Throwing rather than silently producing a long run of Ms is the honest behaviour, and defining the valid domain is part of getting the problem right.

followups.q: Should FromRoman validate its input?
followups.a: For untrusted input, yes. As written it accepts malformed numerals such as IIII or IC and returns a number for them, and it throws a KeyNotFoundException rather than a meaningful error on an unknown character. Proper validation means checking the canonical form, which is most easily done by converting the parsed number back to Roman and comparing against the input. That round-trip check is both simple and complete, and the final test case demonstrates the round trip works.

question: Text justification: format words into lines of exactly maxWidth with even space distribution.

followups.q: Why do the extra spaces go on the left?
followups.a: Because the specification says so, and typographically it reads better than distributing them arbitrarily or on the right. It is enforced by `w - i < extra`, which gives one additional space to the first `extra` gaps. Getting this backwards produces lines of the correct length that differ from the expected output, which is why it is a common source of a solution that looks right and fails. The 'What must be' case exercises it: 3 gaps and 8 spaces gives 3,3,2 rather than 2,3,3.

followups.q: Why are the last line and single-word lines special?
followups.a: Because stretching them would look absurd. A last line with two short words justified to full width would have an enormous gap in the middle, and a single word has no gaps to distribute into at all - dividing by zero gaps would throw. Both are therefore left-justified with the padding on the right. Every real typesetting system does the same, which is why a justified paragraph's final line is always ragged.

followups.q: Why does the test assert every line's length?
followups.a: Because the defining property of justification is that every line is exactly maxWidth, and a solution can produce plausible-looking output with a line one character short. Checking the visible text alone would not catch it, since trailing spaces are invisible. Asserting the invariant rather than the appearance is what makes the test meaningful, and it is the same reasoning as checking prev pointers when flattening a doubly linked list.

question: Reverse only the vowels of a string.

followups.q: Why does the case travel with the letter?
followups.a: Because the swap moves whole characters, not just their vowel identity, so an uppercase A ending up where a lowercase a was stays uppercase. The 'aA' test shows it becoming 'Aa'. Some phrasings of the problem instead ask for the case to stay with the position, which would require detecting the case before swapping and reapplying it afterwards. The two produce different answers, so confirming which is intended is worth a sentence before writing anything.

followups.q: Vowels.IndexOf on every character is a linear scan. Does it matter?
followups.a: The string has ten characters so it is a small constant, and for readability it is hard to beat. A HashSet<char> makes it O(1) with a hash, which for ten items is not obviously faster. The genuinely fastest version is a switch expression, which the compiler turns into a jump table with no allocation at all. For a hot loop that is the version to write, and it is a reasonable answer to give while noting the current one is clearer.

followups.q: What about Unicode vowels such as accented characters?
followups.a: They are not matched, so 'café' would leave the é alone. Whether that is correct depends entirely on the requirement, and the honest answer is that 'vowel' is a linguistic concept rather than a character property, so any implementation encodes an assumption. A broader version would normalise the string and check the base character after stripping combining marks, which is considerably more work and worth doing only if the requirement genuinely covers non-English text.

question: Longest word in a dictionary that can be built one character at a time from other words.

followups.q: Why is checking only the immediate prefix sufficient?
followups.a: Because of the sort order. A word is examined only after every shorter word, so if its immediate prefix is in the buildable set then that prefix itself passed the same check, and so on transitively down to the empty string. Checking every prefix would be correct but redundant and would make it O(total characters) rather than O(n). The induction is what the sort buys, and it is worth stating explicitly because the shortcut looks unsafe without it.

followups.q: Why sort alphabetically as the tie-break?
followups.a: Because the problem specifies the lexicographically smallest answer among equal-length candidates, and sorting that way means the first qualifying word of a given length is already the smallest, so no comparison is needed when updating the best. Without it you would need an explicit tie-break on every update. Pushing the ordering requirement into the sort rather than into the loop is a small simplification that also removes a place to get the comparison backwards.

followups.q: Would a trie be better?
followups.a: It is the other standard solution: insert every word, then DFS from the root following only nodes marked as complete words, tracking the deepest reached. That avoids the sort and is O(total characters), and it naturally handles the lexicographic tie-break by visiting children in order. It uses more memory for the trie structure. For this problem either is fine; the trie generalises better if you also need prefix queries, which is usually why it appears in the same interview.

question: Find the shortest distance between two words in a list of words.

followups.q: Why is tracking only the most recent index sufficient?
followups.a: Because for any new occurrence of one word, the closest occurrence of the other must be the most recent one before it - anything earlier is strictly further away. So older positions can never produce a better answer and need not be kept. That observation is what turns an O(n squared) comparison of all pairs into a single pass with two integers, and it is the same reasoning as in the 'contiguous array' and 'two sum' prefix techniques.

followups.q: Why does the same-word case need separate handling?
followups.a: Because the general branch compares against the other word's last index, and when both words are identical there is no other word - lastA and lastB would track the same thing and the distance would compute as zero. The correct answer is the gap between consecutive occurrences, which means comparing the current index against the previous one before updating it. Solutions that miss this return 0 for the same-word query, which is the standard failure.

followups.q: How would you handle many repeated queries on the same word list?
followups.a: Preprocess once into a dictionary from word to a sorted list of its indices. Each query then merges the two index lists with two pointers, which is O(occurrences of the two words) rather than O(n). For a large corpus queried repeatedly that is a substantial win, and it is exactly how an inverted index supports proximity search in a search engine. It is the standard preprocess-once-query-many trade.

question: Find all duplicates in an array where every element is between 1 and n.

followups.q: Why take the absolute value when reading each element?
followups.a: Because a previous iteration may already have negated it as a mark, and using the negative value directly would compute a negative index and throw. The sign carries the visited flag while the magnitude carries the data, so the two must be separated on every read. It is an in-band encoding, which works here only because the problem guarantees all values are positive and within 1..n; a zero or a negative in the input would break it entirely.

followups.q: Why restore the signs at the end?
followups.a: Because a method named FindDuplicates that silently negates half the caller's array is a nasty surprise, and the restoration costs one extra linear pass. It also makes the method idempotent, so calling it twice gives the same answer, which the last test demonstrates. Without it the second call would report every element as a duplicate. If the caller genuinely does not care, the pass can be dropped and documented, but the default should be to leave the input as you found it.

followups.q: How does this relate to finding the single duplicate in n+1 integers?
followups.a: That variant forbids modifying the array, so the negation trick is unavailable, and it uses Floyd's cycle detection instead: treat values as next pointers, which must form a cycle by the pigeonhole principle, and find its entry. Same O(n) time and O(1) space but no mutation. The pair makes a good illustration that the constraints, not the shape of the data, determine which technique applies.

question: Find the duplicate number in an array of n+1 integers in the range 1..n without modifying it.

followups.q: Why does treating values as pointers guarantee a cycle?
followups.a: Because the sequence starting at index 0 and following x = nums[x] is infinite while the index space is finite, so some index must repeat and the path closes into a cycle. The pigeonhole principle guarantees a duplicated value exists, and that duplicate is what gives two different indices pointing at the same place, making the cycle's entry point rather than the whole path a loop. The values being confined to 1..n is what keeps the traversal in bounds and never reaches index 0 again, which is why index 0 is a safe starting point outside the cycle.

followups.q: Why is this preferred over the marking approach used for finding all duplicates?
followups.a: Purely because of the no-modification constraint. If the array could be altered, negation marking or cyclic sort would be simpler to write and to explain. Floyd's is the answer precisely when the input is read-only and the space must be constant, which is a combination that rules out every simpler technique. It is a good example of constraints selecting the algorithm rather than the data shape doing so.

followups.q: Are there other approaches worth mentioning?
followups.a: Binary search on the value range: for a candidate m, count how many elements are at most m, and if that count exceeds m the duplicate lies in the lower half. That is O(n log n) time and O(1) space, also without modification, and it is easier to explain under pressure than Floyd's. There is also a bit-counting method comparing the input's bit distribution against that of 1..n, which is O(n log n) and rarely worth it. Offering the binary search as the fallback shows range rather than reliance on one trick.

question: Subarray sums divisible by k: count subarrays whose sum is divisible by k.

followups.q: Why does the negative-remainder normalisation matter in practice?
followups.a: Because without it a prefix sum of -3 with k = 5 records remainder -2 while a prefix sum of 2 records 3, and although both represent the same residue class they would never be matched, so valid subarrays are missed and the count comes out too low. It also indexes the array out of bounds with a negative index. Any input containing negative numbers exposes it, which is why the test cases deliberately include them. The same idiom appears in array rotation for the same reason.

followups.q: Why seed the count for remainder zero with one?
followups.a: Because a subarray starting at index 0 whose sum is divisible by k has no earlier prefix to pair with, other than the conceptual empty prefix before the array began, which has sum 0 and therefore remainder 0. Without the seed those subarrays are never counted. It is the identical role played by the `{0: 1}` seed in subarray-sum-equals-k, and forgetting it is the single most common error in both.

followups.q: How does this differ from subarray sum equals k?
followups.a: Structurally they are the same prefix-sum-and-map algorithm; only the key differs. Counting exact sums keys on the prefix value itself and looks up `sum - k`, whereas counting divisible sums keys on the remainder and looks up the same remainder. The remainder version also has bounded space, O(k) rather than O(n), because there are only k possible keys. Recognising that both are instances of 'pair up prefixes satisfying a relation' makes the next variant straightforward.

question: Continuous subarray sum: is there a subarray of length at least two summing to a multiple of k?

followups.q: Why record only the earliest index for each remainder?
followups.a: Because the span between two equal remainders is the qualifying subarray, and to satisfy the length-at-least-two requirement you want the widest possible span. Overwriting with a later index would shrink every span and could reduce a valid length-two subarray to length one, producing a false negative. It is the mirror of problems wanting the shortest span, where you would update to the latest index, and deciding which based on what is being maximised is the reusable part.

followups.q: Why does k equal to zero need a special case?
followups.a: Because taking a modulo by zero throws. When k is zero the question becomes whether a subarray of length at least two sums to exactly zero, so the raw running sum is the key rather than a remainder, and the rest of the algorithm is unchanged. Problem statements vary on whether k can be zero, so it is worth asking; handling it costs one conditional and avoids a crash on an input the statement may permit.

followups.q: Why the double modulo for negative values?
followups.a: Because C# gives the remainder the sign of the dividend, so -3 % 5 is -2 rather than 3, and the two representations of the same residue class would never match. Adding k and taking the modulo again normalises into 0..k-1. It is the same idiom as in array rotation and subarrays-divisible-by-k, and it only manifests when the input contains negatives, which is why such a test case is essential.

question: Partition labels: split a string into as many parts as possible so each letter appears in at most one part.

followups.q: Why does closing at the earliest valid boundary maximise the number of parts?
followups.a: Because any valid partition must place a boundary at or after the current furthest last-occurrence, so closing exactly there is never worse than closing later, and it leaves the maximum remaining string for further splitting. Formally, the greedy choice can be exchanged into any optimal solution without reducing the part count. That exchange argument is what makes the greedy provable rather than merely plausible, and it is the same shape as the argument in activity selection.

followups.q: Suppose you needed the actual substrings, not just their lengths.
followups.a: You already have the boundaries: `partStart` and `partEnd` delimit each part, so a single `s[partStart..(partEnd + 1)]` at the close gives the substring. The problem asks for lengths purely to keep the output compact. It is worth noting that returning substrings allocates memory proportional to the input, whereas returning lengths does not, which matters if the caller only needs to know where to cut.

followups.q: How would you handle a large or unbounded alphabet?
followups.a: Replace the 26-element array with a dictionary from character to last index, which keeps the algorithm identical at the cost of hashing. The complexity stays O(n) time and becomes O(distinct characters) space. For Unicode you would also need to decide whether to work in code points rather than UTF-16 code units, since a surrogate pair split across a boundary would be corrupt, which is the same caveat as in the palindrome and anagram problems.

question: Car pooling: can all trips be completed given a vehicle capacity?

followups.q: Why a difference array rather than incrementing every point in the range?
followups.a: Because incrementing a range of length L costs O(L) per trip, so with many long trips the total is the sum of all trip lengths, which can be far larger than the input. The difference array makes each trip two O(1) updates and defers the accumulation to one final sweep. It is the standard technique for many range updates followed by one read, and the inverse of a prefix-sum array, which serves many range reads after one build.

followups.q: Why subtract at the end index rather than after it?
followups.a: Because passengers alight at the drop-off point, so a trip ending at location 7 and another starting at 7 do not overlap - the seat is free. Subtracting at index 7 makes the occupancy drop before the boarding is added, which is the correct semantics. Subtracting at 8 instead would treat them as overlapping and wrongly reject the back-to-back case, which is exactly what the third test checks. It is the same closed-versus-half-open interval question as in meeting rooms.

followups.q: What if locations were timestamps rather than small integers?
followups.a: An array indexed by location becomes impossible, so you switch to sorting the events: a boarding and an alighting per trip, sorted by position with alightings first at equal positions. Sweeping those events gives the same running occupancy in O(n log n). That is the general sweep-line formulation and it handles unbounded or sparse coordinates, which is why meeting-rooms-II uses it. The difference array is the specialisation that applies when the coordinate space is small and dense.

question: Minimum number of arrows to burst balloons.

followups.q: Why sort by end rather than by start?
followups.a: Because the arrow must be placed somewhere inside the balloon that finishes earliest, and its end is the rightmost such point, so it bursts the most other balloons. Sorting by start would leave you choosing an arrow position without knowing which balloon constrains you most tightly, and a single wide balloon appearing first would mislead the greedy. It is the same reason activity selection sorts by end: the earliest finisher is the least constraining commitment.

followups.q: Why is arrowAt a long rather than an int?
followups.a: Because the coordinates in this problem can span the full int range, and while this particular code only assigns existing coordinates, a version computing midpoints or comparing sums would overflow. It is cheap insurance and signals awareness of the input bounds. The related trap some implementations hit is sorting with a comparator that subtracts two coordinates, which overflows for widely separated values and produces a corrupted sort order; using `OrderBy` with a key avoids that entirely.

followups.q: How does this differ from non-overlapping intervals?
followups.a: They are complementary views of the same sweep. Non-overlapping intervals counts how many intervals can be kept without overlap and removes the rest; this counts how many groups of overlapping intervals exist. One skips overlapping intervals and counts the survivors, the other skips them and counts the groups. Both sort by end and sweep once, and recognising that a whole family of interval problems reduces to that shape is more valuable than either solution alone.

question: Queue reconstruction by height: rebuild a queue from (height, number of taller people in front) pairs.

followups.q: Why does inserting in descending height order work?
followups.a: Because when a person is inserted, every person already in the list is at least as tall as them, so the number of taller-or-equal people in front equals the number of people in front, which is the insertion index. Inserting a shorter person later cannot change that count, since they do not qualify as taller. So each placement is correct at the moment it is made and stays correct. That invariant is the whole proof, and it is what makes an apparently arbitrary greedy provably right.

followups.q: Why break ties by the count ascending?
followups.a: Because among people of equal height, each counts toward the other's total. The one expecting fewer people in front must be placed first; if the larger count went first, inserting the smaller-count person before it would push it back and invalidate its position. Sorting ties the other way produces output that satisfies most entries and quietly breaks on equal heights, which is why the test includes two 7s and two 5s.

followups.q: The list insertion makes this O(n squared). Can it be improved?
followups.a: Yes, with a Fenwick tree or segment tree over the free positions, turning each insertion into a binary search for the k-th remaining empty slot, which gives O(n log n). It is considerably more code and only worth it for large inputs. For interview purposes the O(n squared) version with the correctness argument is the expected answer, and naming the improvement shows you know where the ceiling is without spending the time on it.

question: Boats to save people: minimum boats when each carries at most two people within a weight limit.

followups.q: Why is pairing the heaviest with the lightest optimal?
followups.a: Because the heaviest person must board some boat regardless, so the decision is only whether to fill the remaining seat. If the lightest does not fit, nobody does and the boat is necessarily half empty. If the lightest does fit, pairing them is at least as good as any alternative: the lightest is the easiest person to accommodate later, so spending them here preserves the most flexibility for everyone else. That exchange argument converts a plausible greedy into a proved one.

followups.q: Why does the loop condition use <= rather than <?
followups.a: Because when the two pointers meet there is still one person left to place, and stopping early would leave them without a boat. With light equal to heavy, the condition inside may or may not advance light, but heavy always decrements and a boat is always counted, so the single remaining person is handled correctly either way. Using a strict less-than undercounts by one on any odd-sized input, which the single-person test catches.

followups.q: What if a boat could carry three people?
followups.a: The greedy breaks. With two seats the only question is a yes-or-no pairing, but with three the choice of which two to add to the heaviest is a genuine optimisation, and the exchange argument no longer holds. That variant is a bin-packing problem, which is NP-hard in general, so you would use a heuristic such as first-fit-decreasing and accept an approximation. It is a good illustration that a small relaxation can move a problem from a two-line greedy to intractable.

question: Candy: distribute sweets so higher-rated children get more than their neighbours, minimising the total.

followups.q: Why does the second pass take a maximum rather than assigning directly?
followups.a: Because a child may already hold a larger count from the left-to-right pass, and overwriting would break the left-neighbour constraint that pass established. Consider a peak: it must exceed both neighbours, so it needs the larger of the two requirements. Assigning directly satisfies the right side and violates the left, producing a total that is too small and a distribution that is invalid. The `1,3,2,2,1` case exercises exactly that.

followups.q: Why can't a single pass work?
followups.a: Because each child's requirement depends on both neighbours, and a left-to-right sweep has not yet seen the right neighbour. Any single-direction rule therefore satisfies one constraint and ignores the other. Splitting into two directional passes and combining with a maximum is the standard technique for constraints that look both ways, and it is the same structure as the longest bitonic subsequence and the two-sided version of trapping rain water.

followups.q: Suppose equal ratings had to receive equal sweets.
followups.a: The current rules deliberately allow a lower count for an equal rating, which is why [1,2,2] gives 1,2,1 for a total of 4. Requiring equality would make the constraint graph contain equality edges as well as inequality ones, which the two-pass sweep cannot express, since a chain of equal ratings must be reconciled with whatever the ends demand. You would model it as a graph and propagate, or segment the array into equal-rating runs and solve between them. It is a good example of a small wording change that breaks a neat algorithm.

question: Wiggle subsequence: longest subsequence whose differences alternate in sign.

followups.q: Why does a rise set up = down + 1 rather than up + 1?
followups.a: Because the sequence must alternate, so a rise can only follow a fall. Extending the sequence that already ended on a rise would put two rises together, which is not a wiggle. Taking down + 1 attaches the new rise to the best sequence that ended the opposite way. Writing up + 1 instead silently counts monotonic runs and returns the array length for a sorted input, which the [1,2,3,4,5] test catches immediately.

followups.q: Why do equal adjacent values change nothing?
followups.a: Because a difference of zero is neither a rise nor a fall, so it cannot participate in an alternation and the element is simply skipped. Handling it by falling through both conditions is cleaner than an explicit branch, and it means a long plateau collapses to a single element naturally. The [3,3,3,3] test confirms the answer is 1 rather than 4, which a solution comparing with >= would get wrong.

followups.q: Is the greedy provably optimal here?
followups.a: Yes. At each step the best sequence ending in a given direction is determined entirely by the best sequence ending in the opposite direction, so there is no choice to regret and no need to look ahead. That makes the recurrence exact rather than heuristic, which is why the O(1) rolling version is not an approximation of the DP but identical to it.
