Contrast longest increasing subsequence, where extending is a genuine choice and greedy alone fails.

question: Remove k digits to make the smallest possible number.

followups.q: Why remove a larger digit from an earlier position rather than a larger digit anywhere?
followups.a: Because positional value dominates. Removing a digit shifts everything after it one place left, so eliminating a larger digit from a more significant position reduces the number far more than removing a larger digit later. That is why the stack pops as soon as a smaller digit arrives rather than waiting to find the globally largest digit. The greedy is provable by an exchange argument: any solution not making this removal can be improved by making it.

followups.q: Why can leftover removals be taken from the end?
followups.a: Because if removals remain after the scan, no digit was ever followed by a smaller one, so the sequence is non-decreasing. In a non-decreasing number the largest digits are at the end and also in the least significant positions, so removing from the end is optimal. The `112` with k=1 case shows it: nothing pops during the scan and the trailing 2 is dropped, leaving 11.

followups.q: Why keep leading-zero stripping and the empty case as separate concerns?
followups.a: Because they are different failures. Stripping handles a valid number that happens to begin with zeros, such as 0200 becoming 200, and the loop deliberately stops at the last character so that a genuine single zero survives. The empty case handles removing every digit, which must render as 0 rather than an empty string. Conflating them produces either a stray empty result or a number that loses its final zero, and the `10200` and `10` tests pin both down.

question: Monotone increasing digits: largest number at most n whose digits are non-decreasing.

followups.q: Why scan right to left rather than left to right?
followups.a: Because decrementing a digit can create a new violation with the digit before it. In 332, fixing the 3>2 at the end gives 3 2 9, which now violates at the front. A left-to-right scan would have already passed that position and would return 329, which is not monotone. Scanning backwards means every decrement is re-examined against its own left neighbour on the next iteration. The 332 case is the minimal example that separates the two.

followups.q: Why record fillFrom rather than writing nines immediately?
followups.a: Because a later decrement further left moves the boundary, and nines already written would have to be rewritten. Tracking the leftmost position that needs filling and doing it in one pass afterwards is both simpler and correct. Writing eagerly also destroys the digit values the backwards scan still needs to compare, which would break the cascade detection entirely.

followups.q: Why does 100 give 99 rather than 100?
followups.a: Because 1 > 0 violates the non-decreasing requirement, so the number must come down. Decrementing the 1 gives 0, and filling the rest with nines gives 099, which parses as 99. The leading zero disappearing is exactly right here, since the answer is a number rather than a digit string. It is worth noting that the same code returning a string would need explicit leading-zero handling, which is the kind of detail that differs between phrasings of the problem.

question: Two city scheduling: send n people to each of two cities minimising total cost.

followups.q: Why sort by the difference rather than by the cheaper cost?
followups.a: Because the constraint is that exactly half go to each city, so the question is not who is cheap but who gains most from one city over the other. Someone costing 1 to A and 2 to B is cheap but nearly indifferent; someone costing 1 to A and 100 to B must go to A. Sorting by cost alone would send the first person to A and possibly force the second to B at enormous expense. The last test is built so that cheapest-first picks wrongly.

followups.q: Why is taking the first half provably optimal?
followups.a: By an exchange argument. Suppose an optimal solution sends someone with a larger A-advantage to B and someone with a smaller one to A. Swapping them changes the total by the difference of their differences, which is non-positive, so the swap cannot make things worse. Repeating the swap transforms any optimal solution into the sorted one, so the sorted assignment is optimal. That argument is what elevates this from a plausible heuristic to a proof.

followups.q: How would this change for three cities?
followups.a: The difference ordering no longer exists, because each person now has three costs and no single scalar captures their preference. It becomes an assignment problem with capacity constraints, solvable in polynomial time with min-cost max-flow or the Hungarian algorithm, but not by sorting. That jump is worth naming: the two-city case is special because the difference reduces two numbers to one, and with three numbers there is nothing to sort by.

question: Game of Life: compute the next generation in place.

followups.q: Why does the two-bit encoding work?
followups.a: Because the two states live in different bits and never interfere. Writing the new state into bit 1 leaves bit 0 untouched, so every subsequent neighbour count that masks with `& 1` still sees the original generation regardless of how many cells have already been processed. The final shift promotes every cell at once, which is the atomic swap that a simultaneous update requires. It is a neat use of spare capacity in an int that is only holding a boolean.

followups.q: What if the board were infinite, as Conway intended?
followups.a: An array no longer works, so you store only the live cells in a hash set of coordinates. Each generation, count neighbours for every live cell and for every dead cell adjacent to a live one, since no other cell can change. That makes the cost proportional to the population rather than to the area, which is what makes large sparse patterns feasible. Serious implementations go further with HashLife, which memoises repeated subpatterns and can simulate astronomical generation counts.

followups.q: How would you parallelise this?
followups.a: The computation is naturally data-parallel, since each cell's next state depends only on the previous generation, so rows or tiles can be processed independently. The catch is the in-place encoding: it is safe here only because the old state survives in bit 0, so concurrent readers still see consistent data. A double-buffered version is simpler to reason about under parallelism and usually preferred, trading O(rc) extra memory for an obviously correct memory model.

question: Diagonal traverse of a matrix.

followups.q: Why do cells on a diagonal share row + col?
followups.a: Because moving one step up-right decreases the row by one and increases the column by one, leaving the sum unchanged. That makes row + col a natural identifier for the anti-diagonal, exactly as row - col identifies the main diagonal - which is the same pair of identities used in N-Queens to detect attacks. Recognising that one arithmetic expression names a whole diagonal is what turns a fiddly walk into a simple grouping.

followups.q: Where do the startRow and endRow bounds come from?
followups.a: The column is d - row and must be within 0 to cols-1, which gives row at least d - cols + 1. The row itself must be within 0 to rows-1, giving row at most d and at least 0. Combining them produces the two clamps. Deriving them rather than guessing matters because an off-by-one here reads outside the matrix, and the failure only appears on non-square inputs, which is why the single-row and single-column tests are present.

followups.q: Could you avoid the reverse by walking each direction directly?
followups.a: Yes, by computing the starting cell for each direction and stepping with the appropriate delta, which avoids building and reversing a list. It is marginally faster and noticeably harder to get right, since the start point differs depending on whether the diagonal has hit the right edge yet. Collecting then reversing keeps the bound logic in one place, and the reverse is O(length of that diagonal), so the total remains linear.

question: Valid Sudoku: is a partially filled 9x9 board valid?

followups.q: Explain the box index formula.
followups.a: Integer division by three collapses the nine rows into three bands and the nine columns into three stacks, so `r / 3` and `c / 3` each give 0, 1 or 2. Multiplying the band by three and adding the stack numbers the boxes 0 to 8 in reading order. It is the same flattening as converting two-dimensional coordinates to a one-dimensional index, and deriving it rather than recalling it is quick once you see that it is just a base-three pair.

followups.q: Why bitmasks rather than HashSets?
followups.a: Because there are only nine possible digits, so a single int holds the whole set with one bit per digit, and membership is one AND rather than a hash lookup. It removes 27 allocations and all hashing. For a fixed nine-digit alphabet it is clearly better; for a generalised n by n Sudoku with large n you would move to a bitset or a HashSet. The readability cost is small and the comment carries the intent.

followups.q: How would you extend this to actually solving the puzzle?
followups.a: Backtracking: find an empty cell, try each digit that does not conflict, recurse, and undo on failure. The validity check here becomes the constraint test inside the loop, and the bitmasks become incrementally maintained state rather than being rebuilt. The big win is ordering: always filling the most constrained cell first, the minimum-remaining-values heuristic, turns a slow search into a fast one. That is the natural escalation once the validator works.

question: 01 matrix: distance of each cell to the nearest zero.

followups.q: Why use -1 as the unvisited marker rather than a separate visited array?
followups.a: Because 0 is a legitimate distance, for the zero cells themselves, so it cannot double as 'unvisited'. Using -1 keeps one array instead of two and makes the check a single comparison. It is a safe in-band sentinel here because distances are never negative, which is the test any such sentinel must pass. Using int.MaxValue would also work and is what you would need if -1 were meaningful data.

followups.q: Could this be solved with dynamic programming instead?
followups.a: Yes, with two passes. Sweep top-left to bottom-right taking the minimum of the cell above and to the left plus one, then bottom-right to top-left taking the minimum of below and right plus one. That is O(rc) with no queue and is often faster in practice due to sequential memory access. It works because the shortest path in a four-directional grid can be decomposed into these two directional sweeps, and it is a genuinely good alternative answer.

followups.q: What if the distance were Euclidean rather than Manhattan?
followups.a: BFS no longer applies, because diagonal steps would cost the square root of two rather than one, so the graph becomes weighted and Dijkstra would be needed. For a true Euclidean distance transform there are specialised O(rc) algorithms operating per row and per column using parabola intersections. It is worth flagging that 'nearest' depends entirely on the metric, and that the four-directional assumption is what makes the cheap BFS valid.

question: Flood fill: change the colour of a connected region starting from a pixel.

followups.q: Why is the same-colour check essential rather than an optimisation?
followups.a: Because without it the algorithm does not terminate. A cell recoloured to the original colour still satisfies the 'matches the original' condition, so neighbours keep re-enqueuing each other indefinitely and the queue grows without bound. It is not a performance issue but an infinite loop, and it is the single most common failure in this problem. The second test exists to pin it down.

followups.q: Why BFS rather than the recursive DFS most people write?
followups.a: Because a large uniform region recurses once per cell, so a 1000 by 1000 image of one colour would attempt a million stack frames and overflow. .NET cannot catch a StackOverflowException, so the process dies. BFS with an explicit queue has no such limit, using heap memory proportional to the frontier instead. For small grids either is fine, and for anything user-supplied the iterative version is the responsible choice.

followups.q: How does a real paint-bucket tool differ from this?
followups.a: Several ways. It usually works on a tolerance rather than exact equality, so nearby shades are included, which means the 'matches the original' test becomes a distance in colour space. It often needs anti-aliased edges rather than a hard boundary. And for large images the scanline fill is preferred, which fills whole horizontal runs at a time and enqueues only the spans above and below, dramatically reducing the number of queue operations and improving cache locality.

question: Shortest path in a binary matrix with eight-directional movement.

followups.q: Why does BFS give the shortest path here but not in general?
followups.a: Because every move costs exactly one, including diagonals, so the number of steps is the distance and BFS explores in distance order. If diagonal moves cost the square root of two, as they would for true Euclidean distance, the graph becomes weighted and BFS would no longer be correct - you would need Dijkstra. The problem's definition of a step as one cell regardless of direction is what makes the cheap algorithm valid, and that assumption is worth stating.

followups.q: Why mark cells on enqueue rather than on dequeue?
followups.a: Because a cell can be reached from several neighbours, and marking only when it is processed lets it be enqueued multiple times before the first is handled. The queue then grows beyond the grid size and the algorithm does redundant work. Marking at enqueue guarantees each cell enters exactly once, which is what keeps it linear. It is the same correction as in number-of-islands and rotting-oranges.

followups.q: The code mutates the caller's grid. Is that acceptable?
followups.a: It avoids allocating a visited array, which is the usual justification, but it is a real side effect: a caller reusing the grid afterwards sees every reachable cell marked as blocked. For an interview it is worth flagging as a deliberate trade. In production I would allocate a separate visited array, or restore the grid before returning, since a method named ShortestPath that destroys its input is a surprise the type signature does not communicate.

question: Implement a BST iterator with next and hasNext in average O(1).

followups.q: Why is this amortised O(1) when one Next can push many nodes?
followups.a: Because each node is pushed exactly once and popped exactly once over the entire traversal, so the total work across n calls is 2n stack operations. A single call that pushes a long spine has effectively prepaid for the subsequent calls that pop it without pushing. Averaged over the traversal that is constant. It is the same accounting as the two-stack queue, and stating it as amortised rather than worst-case is the precise answer.

followups.q: Why O(h) space rather than materialising the traversal?
followups.a: Because the stack only ever holds the path from the root to the current node plus pending right subtrees, which is bounded by the height. For a balanced tree that is logarithmic, so a million-node tree needs about twenty stack entries instead of a million list entries. The materialised version is simpler and is the right choice if the traversal will be replayed, but for a single forward pass the stack is strictly better.

followups.q: How would you add a Previous operation?
followups.a: The single stack cannot go backwards, because popping discards the path. You would keep a second stack of already-visited nodes, moving nodes between the two as the cursor advances and retreats, which is the same two-stack technique as a browser history. Alternatively, if the tree has parent pointers, the in-order predecessor is computable directly and no extra state is needed. Which applies depends on whether you control the node type.

question: Delete a node from a binary search tree.

followups.q: Why must the replacement be the predecessor or the successor specifically?
followups.a: Because the BST invariant requires everything in the left subtree to be smaller and everything in the right to be larger. Only two values in the tree sit immediately adjacent to the deleted one in sorted order, and either can occupy the position without violating that for any other node. Any other value would be on the wrong side of something. It is a nice example of a constraint that leaves exactly two valid choices rather than one.

followups.q: Why is the recursive delete of the successor guaranteed to terminate quickly?
followups.a: Because the in-order successor is the leftmost node of the right subtree, so by construction it has no left child, which means the recursion lands in the zero-or-one-child case immediately. That makes the two-children case cost O(h) for the search plus O(1) for the fix-up rather than recursing indefinitely. Understanding that the hard case reduces to an easy one is the point of the design.

followups.q: Copying the value rather than relinking the node - any downside?
followups.a: Yes. Any external reference to the successor node now sees a different value, and any reference to the deleted node sees the successor's value while believing it holds the old one. If nodes carry identity or are referenced elsewhere, such as from an index, that is a real bug. Relinking the successor node into position instead is more pointer work but preserves identity, which is what a production implementation would do.

followups.q: Does repeated deletion unbalance the tree?
followups.a: Yes, and it is a known asymmetry: always taking the successor biases the tree toward becoming left-heavy over many deletions, because the right subtree is repeatedly shortened. Alternating between predecessor and successor mitigates it. A self-balancing tree such as AVL or red-black rebalances after deletion instead, which is why production ordered collections use them rather than a plain BST.

question: Path sum III: count paths summing to a target, starting and ending anywhere downward.

followups.q: Why must the prefix be removed as the recursion unwinds?
followups.a: Because a valid path is a single downward chain, so a prefix recorded while descending the left subtree must not be visible while descending the right. Leaving it in the map would count paths that jump between branches, which do not exist. The decrement restores the map to exactly the ancestors of the current node, which is the invariant the algorithm depends on. Omitting it produces counts that are too high and only on trees with branching, so a linear test tree would not catch it.

followups.q: Why seed the map with {0: 1}?
followups.a: Because a path starting at the root has no ancestor prefix to subtract, and the conceptual empty prefix before the root has sum zero. Without the seed, any path beginning at the root is missed entirely. It is the same seeding as in subarray-sum-equals-k, and forgetting it is the most common error in both. The single-node test with target equal to its value pins it down.

followups.q: Why accumulate the running sum in a long?
followups.a: Because the path sum can exceed int range even when individual node values do not, on a deep tree with large values. An overflowed prefix wraps and can coincidentally match a lookup, producing a wrong count with no error. Widening the accumulator costs nothing and removes a failure mode that only appears at scale. The map key is widened to match, since the two must compare consistently.

question: House robber III: maximum sum from a binary tree with no two directly connected nodes.

followups.q: Why return a pair rather than the single best value?
followups.a: Because a parent cannot decide from its child's best alone - it needs to know the best under the constraint that the child was not taken. Returning only the maximum loses that, so the parent would have to descend to the grandchildren to recompute it, which makes the algorithm exponential through repeated work. Carrying both states upward keeps each node visited once. It is the same return-a-richer-value technique as in tree diameter and maximum path sum.

followups.q: How is this the same as the array version of house robber?
followups.a: Identical recurrence, different traversal. The array version keeps two rolling values, the best including the current house and the best excluding it, and each new house combines them. Here the two values are returned up from children rather than carried along a line, because the structure branches. Recognising that the array, circular and tree variants are one recurrence over three shapes is what makes the third one quick to write.

followups.q: Why does the second example give 9 rather than taking the root?
followups.a: Because taking the root at 3 forbids both children, leaving only the grandchildren 1, 3 and 1 for a total of 8. Skipping the root allows both children, 4 and 5, for 9. It is the case that proves greedy fails: the root is not the largest value but the choice still propagates two levels. Including an example where the obvious local choice loses is what makes a test meaningful rather than confirmatory.

question: Find all nodes at distance k from a target node in a binary tree.

followups.q: Why build a parent map rather than searching downward?
followups.a: Because nodes at distance k can be above the target, or in a sibling subtree reached by going up and then down again. In the example, distance 2 from node 5 includes node 1, which is reached by going up to the root and down the other side. A downward-only search finds 7 and 4 and misses it entirely. The parent map converts the tree into an undirected graph, at which point distance means what it normally means.

followups.q: Why is the visited set essential rather than merely an optimisation?
followups.a: Because once parent links exist, stepping from a node to its parent and back to the same node is a legal two-step walk, so the traversal would oscillate forever. In a plain tree BFS there are no cycles and the set can be omitted. Adding parent edges introduces them, which is the price of making the tree undirected. It is a good illustration that a data structure's guarantees change when you add edges to it.

followups.q: Could you avoid the parent map?
followups.a: Yes, with a single recursion that returns the distance from each node to the target and handles the case where the target is in the other subtree, adding nodes at the appropriate depth as the recursion unwinds. It is O(n) with O(h) space rather than O(n) space, so it is genuinely better, but the logic is considerably more delicate. The parent-map version is the one to write first because its correctness is obvious, and the recursive version is the optimisation to mention.

question: Vertical order traversal of a binary tree.

followups.q: Why is sorting by value necessary as the third key?
followups.a: Because two nodes can occupy the same column and the same row while being in different subtrees, as 5 and 6 do in the second example - 6 is the right child of 2 and 5 is the left child of 3, both at column 0, row 2. The problem specifies they are ordered by value, so 5 precedes 6. A BFS that relies on insertion order would emit 6 first, since the left subtree is visited first. It is the detail that separates this from the simpler column-grouping problem.

followups.q: Would a BFS be better than collecting and sorting?
followups.a: BFS gives rows in order for free, so you would only need to sort within a row-and-column group rather than globally, which is a smaller sort. But you still need that sort for the value tie-break, so the code does not get simpler. Collecting everything and sorting once is easier to reason about and the O(n log n) is the same either way. For a very large tree the BFS version has better constants.

followups.q: What is the difference between this and the top view of a tree?
followups.a: The top view takes only the first node encountered in each column, which requires BFS specifically, because DFS could reach a deeper node in a column before a shallower one and record the wrong value. Vertical order takes every node in every column. So one needs a level-order guarantee and the other does not, which is a neat example of the traversal choice being forced by the requirement rather than being a matter of taste.

question: Count good nodes in a binary tree: nodes with no larger value on the path from the root.

followups.q: Why is the comparison >= rather than >?
followups.a: Because the definition is that no node on the path is *larger*, so an equal value still qualifies - there is nothing strictly greater before it. The second example makes this concrete: a 3 beneath a 3 is good, giving 3 rather than 2. Using a strict greater-than undercounts on any tree with repeated values along a path, which is easy to miss if the test data has distinct values throughout.

followups.q: Why seed with int.MinValue rather than the root's value?
followups.a: So the root is counted without a special case, since any value is at least int.MinValue. Seeding with the root's value would also work here but would need the root handled separately, and seeding with 0 would break on trees containing negative values, which the last test exercises. Choosing a seed outside the possible data range is the general rule, and it is the same reasoning as the sentinel discussion in BST validation.

followups.q: Could this be done iteratively?
followups.a: Yes, with an explicit stack holding node-and-maximum pairs, which removes the recursion depth limit. The recursion is only as deep as the tree, so for a balanced tree it is fine, but a degenerate tree of a million nodes would overflow. Since the state passed down is a single integer, the iterative version is genuinely simple here, which is not always true of pre-order algorithms carrying richer state.

question: Check whether one binary tree is a subtree of another.

followups.q: Why do the null markers matter in the serialisation approach?
followups.a: Because without them, different trees can serialise identically. A node with only a left child and a node with only a right child would both produce the parent followed by the one value, so a subtree could be found that has the wrong shape. The markers make the structure explicit, which is the same reason serialise-and-deserialise needs them to round-trip. It is the difference between encoding the values and encoding the tree.

followups.q: Why does the serialisation prefix every value with a comma?
followups.a: To prevent a value matching inside a larger number. Without a separator, a subtree rooted at 2 would be found inside a tree containing 12, since the substring search sees the digits. The leading comma makes every token delimited, so the match is on whole values. It is the same delimiter hazard as in the group-anagrams count key, where 1 and 11 concatenate ambiguously.

followups.q: Which version would you ship?
followups.a: The recursive one, in most cases. It is shorter, allocates nothing, and its worst case only materialises when the candidate root value is extremely common in the larger tree. The serialisation version allocates two strings proportional to the trees and relies on the substring search being linear, which .NET's Contains is in practice but is not contractually guaranteed. If the same subtree were tested against many trees, precomputing its serialisation once would tip the balance.

question: Recover a binary search tree where exactly two nodes were swapped.

followups.q: Why does first use ??= while second is assigned unconditionally?
followups.a: Because the two cases need different behaviour and this expresses both with one rule. With two separate inversions, first must stay pinned to the earlier element of the first inversion while second advances to the later element of the second. With a single inversion, the same line sets first to the earlier element and second to the later one in the same step. Writing two branches for the adjacent and non-adjacent cases also works but is easy to get subtly wrong.

followups.q: Can this be done in O(1) space?
followups.a: Yes, with Morris traversal, which threads unused right pointers to walk in order without a stack and restores them afterwards. That gives genuine O(1) auxiliary space and is the answer if the interviewer pushes on it. The cost is that the tree is temporarily mutated during traversal, so it is unusable if anything else may read the tree concurrently, and the code is considerably harder to verify by eye.

followups.q: Why swap the values rather than relinking the nodes?
followups.a: Because relinking two arbitrary nodes in a tree means fixing up to six pointers including both parents, and the nodes may be ancestor and descendant of each other, which needs special handling. Swapping values is two assignments and is correct for the problem as stated. The caveat is the usual one: any external reference to a specific node now sees a different value, so if nodes carry identity the relink is the honest fix.

question: Convert a BST to a greater tree where each node holds the sum of all greater values.

followups.q: Why reverse in-order rather than collecting and sorting?
followups.a: Because the BST already encodes the order, so a traversal in the right direction gives descending values for free in O(n). Collecting into a list, sorting and writing back would be O(n log n) and O(n) space for no benefit. It is a good illustration that the structure's invariant is the thing you are paying for, and using a general-purpose sort on a BST discards it.

followups.q: Why pass the running sum by ref rather than using a field?
followups.a: To keep the method free of shared mutable state, so two threads converting different trees cannot corrupt each other, and so the dependency is visible in the signature. A private field would work single-threaded but makes the method non-reentrant. The alternative is to return the running total from each call and thread it through, which is purely functional and arguably cleaner at the cost of slightly noisier code. It is the same choice as passing best by ref in tree diameter.

followups.q: The negatives case leaves the tree unchanged. Why?
followups.a: For values -1, 0, 1 the sums happen to be 0, -1 and 1 again, which coincidentally matches the input. It is worth including precisely because a coincidence like that can mask a bug in the other direction, and because it confirms negatives are handled rather than assumed away. Checking the in-order sequence rather than individual nodes is what makes the test meaningful here.

question: Count the number of structurally unique BSTs with n nodes.

followups.q: Why is count[0] equal to 1 rather than 0?
followups.a: Because it represents the empty tree, and there is exactly one way to arrange no nodes. Setting it to 0 would make every product zero and the whole table collapse. It is the same convention as the empty product being 1 and 0 factorial being 1, and it is what lets a root with no left child contribute its right subtree's count unchanged rather than annihilating it.

followups.q: Where else does this sequence appear?
followups.a: These are the Catalan numbers, and they count a surprising range of things: balanced bracket sequences, which is why generate-parentheses has the same answers; triangulations of a convex polygon; the ways to parenthesise a product; and monotonic lattice paths below a diagonal. Recognising the sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42 is often the fastest route to an answer, because if a problem produces those counts it almost certainly has the same recursive structure.

followups.q: Why return long?
followups.a: Because Catalan numbers grow roughly 4^n, so the count exceeds int range at n of 19 and long range around n of 33. The test at n of 30 makes that visible. Returning int would silently wrap and produce a plausible negative number, which is worse than an exception. Where n could be larger still, you would compute modulo a prime, which is what competitive problem statements specify for exactly this reason.

question: Cheapest flights within k stops.

followups.q: Why is the snapshot essential?
followups.a: Because relaxing against the live array lets a distance improved earlier in the same round be used again later in that round, chaining two flights into one round. The stop limit would then be silently exceeded and the answer too cheap. The first test exposes it: with one stop allowed, the answer must be 700 via 0-1-3, and a version without the snapshot finds 400 via three flights. It is the difference between bounding path length and bounding iterations.

followups.q: Why not Dijkstra?
followups.a: Because Dijkstra settles a node once, at its cheapest cost, and discards any more expensive route to it - but a more expensive route with fewer stops may be the only one that can reach the destination within the limit. The constraint makes cost alone an insufficient state. A modified Dijkstra keyed on the pair (node, stops used) does work and is often faster in practice, since it explores in cost order, but it needs the state widened to include the stop count.

followups.q: Why k+1 rounds rather than k?
followups.a: Because k stops means k intermediate airports, which is k+1 flights. A direct flight is zero stops and one flight, so with k of 0 the loop must still run once. Off-by-one here gives answers that are correct for larger k and wrong at the boundary, which is why the test includes k of 0 explicitly. Restating the constraint in terms of edges rather than stops before writing the loop avoids the mistake.

question: Redundant connection: find the edge that can be removed to make a tree.

followups.q: Why does the first cycle-closing edge happen to be the answer the problem wants?
followups.a: Because the input is guaranteed to contain exactly one redundant edge, so only one edge can ever close a cycle during the scan. The problem phrases it as 'the last edge in input order' to disambiguate in general, but with a single cycle the first edge found is also the last such edge, since there is only one. If there were several, you would continue scanning and keep the most recent, which is a one-line change.

followups.q: Why union-find rather than DFS?
followups.a: Because union-find processes edges incrementally, which matches the problem exactly: you want the edge that closes a cycle at the moment it is added, which is precisely what a failed union reports. A DFS would find that a cycle exists but not naturally identify which edge in input order created it, so you would need extra bookkeeping. It is a good example of choosing the structure that answers the question directly rather than one that answers a related question.

followups.q: How does the directed version differ?
followups.a: Considerably. In a directed graph the redundant edge might create a node with two parents rather than a cycle, or both, so you first look for a node with in-degree two and try removing each of its incoming edges, checking whether the rest forms a valid tree. That is redundant-connection II and is noticeably harder, because union-find alone cannot distinguish a cycle from a two-parent violation. Naming that difference is worth doing if the interviewer escalates.

question: Accounts merge: group email accounts belonging to the same person.

followups.q: Why union emails rather than accounts?
followups.a: Because the email is the identity evidence and an account is just a bundle of them. Unioning accounts directly would require first working out which accounts overlap, which is the problem itself. Unioning emails makes the overlap emerge automatically: two accounts sharing any email end up with their emails in one component. It is a good example of choosing the right thing to union, which is usually the atom of identity rather than the container.

followups.q: Why can the name be taken from any email in the group?
followups.a: Because the problem guarantees that accounts sharing an email belong to the same person, so every email in a component maps to the same name. That guarantee is what makes the lookup safe. Note the converse does not hold: two people with the same name and no shared email stay separate, which the two Johns in the test demonstrate. Confusing the name for the identity is the modelling error the question is probing.

followups.q: What would this look like in a real identity system?
followups.a: The same connected-components idea, but the evidence is richer and weaker: shared email, shared device, shared payment method, shared address. Each carries a confidence rather than a certainty, so a plain union-find over-merges - one shared household device would fuse two families. Real systems use weighted evidence with a threshold, keep the merge reversible, and require human review above a certain blast radius, because an incorrect merge of two customers is far more damaging than a missed one.

question: Evaluate division: answer queries like a/c given ratios a/b and b/c.

followups.q: Why does x / x return -1 while a / a returns 1?
followups.a: Because the answer must be derivable from the given equations, and an unknown variable gives no basis for any claim about it - not even that it equals itself, since it might be zero or undefined. A variable that appears in the input is known to be a well-defined non-zero quantity, so dividing it by itself is 1. That asymmetry is the detail most implementations miss, and it is why the membership check precedes the search rather than being folded into it.

followups.q: Why union-find rather than DFS, if the queries are numerous?
followups.a: A weighted union-find stores each node's ratio to its component root, so a query becomes two Find operations and a division, which is near-constant after path compression. That beats a DFS per query when there are many queries over a static equation set. The complication is that path compression must update the stored weights as it rewires, which is more delicate than the plain version. For a handful of queries the DFS is simpler and fast enough.

followups.q: What about floating-point accumulation over a long path?
followups.a: Multiplying many ratios accumulates rounding error, so a long chain can drift measurably from the exact value. For interview inputs it is irrelevant, but in a real unit-conversion system you would store ratios as exact rationals or convert via a canonical base unit rather than chaining, which bounds the error to one multiplication. It is the same reasoning as converting currencies through a base rather than composing pairwise rates.

question: Minimum height trees: find all roots that minimise tree height.

followups.q: Why can there be at most two answers?
followups.a: Because a tree's centre is defined by its longest path, the diameter. If the diameter has an even number of edges there is a single middle node; if odd, there are two adjacent middle nodes. No other configuration is possible, so the peeling can safely stop at two. If the algorithm ever left three, that would indicate a bug or a graph that is not a tree, which is worth knowing as a sanity check.

followups.q: Why peel leaves rather than computing the height from every node?
followups.a: Because computing the height rooted at each node is O(n) per node and O(n squared) overall, which is fine for small graphs and hopeless for large ones. Peeling touches each node and edge once, so it is linear. The insight is that you do not need the heights at all - you only need to identify the centre, and peeling finds it directly. That reframing from 'evaluate every candidate' to 'construct the answer' is the substance of the problem.

followups.q: Why is n of 2 or fewer special-cased?
followups.a: Because with two nodes both have degree 1, so both are leaves and the peeling loop would never start, yet both are valid answers. With one node the degree is 0 so it is never added to the initial leaf list at all. Returning all nodes directly for those cases is simpler than trying to make the general loop handle them, and it matches the definition: with two nodes, rooting at either gives height 1.

question: Reconstruct an itinerary from a list of tickets using every ticket once.

followups.q: Why does the plain greedy fail?
followups.a: Because taking the lexicographically smallest destination at every step can lead into a dead end while tickets remain elsewhere. The third test shows it: from JFK, taking KUL first strands you there with the NRT ticket unused, even though JFK-NRT-JFK-KUL uses everything. Hierholzer's handles it by treating a dead end as the *end* of the route rather than a failure, backing up and building the itinerary in reverse. The stranded airport is genuinely last, which is why prepending is correct.

followups.q: Why is the route built in reverse?
followups.a: Because an airport is only added when it has no unused tickets left, which means nothing can follow it in the final route. So the first airport added is the last one visited. Popping into a list and reversing at the end is the natural expression of that. Trying to build it forwards requires knowing in advance which branch is the dead end, which is exactly the information the algorithm is discovering.

followups.q: When does an Eulerian path exist at all?
followups.a: For a directed graph, when it is connected over the edges and at most one vertex has out-degree exceeding in-degree by one (the start), at most one has in-degree exceeding out-degree by one (the end), and all others are balanced. The problem guarantees a valid itinerary exists, so the check is omitted. Adding it would be the responsible thing in production, since without it the algorithm silently returns a partial route rather than reporting that the tickets cannot be used.

question: Find the critical connections (bridges) in a network.

followups.q: Why is the comparison strictly greater rather than greater-or-equal?
followups.a: Because equality means the child's subtree can reach back to the parent itself, which is only possible through a cycle containing the edge - so removing it leaves the graph connected and it is not a bridge. Strictly greater means the subtree cannot reach even as far back as the parent, so the edge is the only link. Using >= would report every edge in a cycle as critical, which the triangle test immediately exposes.

followups.q: Why must the parent edge be skipped?
followups.a: Because the edge you arrived on always leads back to a node with an earlier discovery time, so counting it would make every node's reachable minimum equal its parent's, and no edge would ever satisfy the bridge condition. Skipping it is what makes back edges meaningful. The subtlety is that skipping by parent *node* is wrong when parallel edges exist, since a second edge to the same parent genuinely is a cycle; skipping by edge identity handles that correctly.

followups.q: What is the practical use of finding bridges?
followups.a: Identifying single points of failure in a network: a bridge is a link whose loss partitions the system. The same algorithm with a slightly different condition finds articulation points, which are the equivalent for nodes rather than edges. In distributed systems it tells you which connections need redundancy, and in dependency graphs it identifies modules whose removal would disconnect parts of the codebase, which is a useful signal when planning a refactor.

question: Walls and gates: fill each empty room with the distance to the nearest gate.

followups.q: Why is multi-source BFS correct rather than just convenient?
followups.a: Because BFS explores in order of distance from the frontier, and seeding with every gate makes the initial frontier the set of all gates at distance zero. The first time any room is reached is therefore by the shortest path from whichever gate is nearest. It is not an approximation of running k separate searches and taking the minimum - it computes the same result in one pass. The same argument applies to rotting oranges and the 01-matrix problem.

followups.q: Why does checking for the sentinel double as a visited check?
followups.a: Because a room is only ever written once, when it is first reached, and writing it changes it from the sentinel to a real distance. So the condition 'still equals the sentinel' means exactly 'not yet reached'. That removes the need for a separate visited array, which is neat, but it depends on the sentinel being outside the range of real distances - int.MaxValue is safe because no path can be that long.

followups.q: What if the gates could be added or removed over time?
followups.a: Recomputing the whole grid on every change is O(rc) and may be fine for a small grid. Adding a gate only ever decreases distances, so you can BFS from just the new gate and stop early wherever the existing distance is already smaller, which is usually much cheaper. Removing a gate is the hard direction, because distances can increase and you cannot know how far the effect spreads without recomputation - which is a general property of shortest-path maintenance under edge deletion.

question: Open the lock: minimum turns to reach a target combination avoiding deadends.

followups.q: Why seed the visited set with the deadends?
followups.a: Because a deadend is a state you may never occupy, which is operationally identical to having already visited it - both mean 'do not enqueue this'. Merging them into one set removes a second membership check from the inner loop, which runs eighty thousand times. It also makes the start check natural: if 0000 is a deadend the search cannot begin at all, which is why that case is tested before the loop rather than discovered inside it.

followups.q: Why check the target before starting rather than inside the loop?
followups.a: Because the loop increments the turn counter before examining a level, so a target equal to the start would be reported as taking turns when it takes none. Checking up front returns 0 correctly. It is the same class of off-by-one as in jump game II, where the loop must stop before the last index, and it only shows up on the degenerate input that people forget to test.

followups.q: Could this be made faster?
followups.a: Bidirectional BFS, searching from both the start and the target and stopping when the frontiers meet, roughly square-roots the number of states explored. With only 10,000 states the plain version is already instantaneous, so it is not worth it here, but the technique is the standard answer when the state space is large - it is what makes word ladder tractable on a big dictionary. Naming it shows you know the ceiling without spending effort you do not need.

question: Number of provinces: count connected components given an adjacency matrix.

followups.q: Why is this O(n squared) rather than O(V + E)?
followups.a: Because the input is an adjacency matrix, so finding a city's neighbours means scanning a whole row of n entries regardless of how many are actually connected. Every city is scanned once, giving n squared. With an adjacency list the same algorithm would be O(V + E), which for a sparse graph is far better. The representation, not the algorithm, sets the bound here - which is why the choice of representation is itself a design decision.

followups.q: Would union-find be better?
followups.a: It is equally valid and equally O(n squared) here, since you still have to read every matrix entry to know which pairs to union. Union-find wins when edges arrive incrementally and the count must stay current, because it absorbs a new edge in near-constant time while a traversal would have to restart. For a single static query over a matrix, the traversal is simpler and has no extra structure to maintain.

followups.q: Why does the diagonal need no special handling?
followups.a: Because connected[i][i] is always 1, so the scan sees the city as its own neighbour, finds it already visited, and skips it. The visited check absorbs it naturally. Writing an explicit skip for the diagonal would be harmless but redundant. It is a small example of an invariant in the input making a special case unnecessary, which is worth noticing rather than defending against.

question: Satisfiability of equality equations such as a==b and b!=c.

followups.q: Why must all equalities be processed before any inequality?
followups.a: Because equality is transitive and the full set of merges determines which variables are forced equal. Checking an inequality early evaluates it against an incomplete partition, so a later equality that creates the contradiction is missed. The last test is built for this: 'a!=c' appears first and only becomes contradictory once 'b==c' and 'a==b' have been applied. Interleaved processing returns true, which is wrong.

followups.q: Why does a!=a fail without any equality at all?
followups.a: Because a variable is trivially in its own component, so Find returns the same root for both sides and the inequality is violated immediately. It is a nice property of the formulation: the self-contradiction needs no special case, since the union-find already encodes that everything equals itself. A solution that only compared distinct variables would miss it, which is why it is worth testing.

followups.q: How does this generalise beyond equality and inequality?
followups.a: Adding ordering constraints such as a < b turns it into a different problem: union-find handles equivalence relations, which are symmetric, but ordering is antisymmetric and needs a directed graph with cycle detection instead - a cycle in the less-than graph is the contradiction. Mixing both, which is what a real constraint solver faces, requires combining union-find for the equalities with a topological check over the merged components. That layering is the standard structure of a congruence-closure solver.

question: Path with maximum probability between two nodes.

followups.q: Why is Dijkstra valid for probabilities when it fails for negative weights?
followups.a: Because what Dijkstra actually requires is that extending a path never improves it, so a settled node can never be beaten later. With additive non-negative weights, adding an edge increases cost. With probabilities in [0,1], multiplying by another factor decreases the product. Both satisfy the monotonicity. A probability above 1 would break it exactly as a negative weight does, which is why the closed interval matters rather than merely the sign.

followups.q: Could you take logarithms instead?
followups.a: Yes, and it is a common trick: taking the negative logarithm turns products into sums and maximisation into minimisation, so you can use a standard Dijkstra unchanged. The catch is a probability of zero, whose logarithm is negative infinity, and the accumulation of floating-point error across many logarithms and one final exponentiation. For this problem the direct multiplication is simpler and more accurate, but the log transform is worth knowing because it is how many multiplicative optimisations are made additive.

followups.q: Why the settled array rather than decrease-key?
followups.a: Because .NET's PriorityQueue cannot update an element's priority in place, so the standard workaround is to push a new entry at the improved probability and skip any pop for an already-settled node. The heap can then hold up to E entries rather than V, which costs memory but performs well. It is the same lazy-deletion pattern as in the shortest-path and network-delay problems, and it is worth naming as a deliberate choice rather than leaving it unexplained.

question: Minimum cost climbing stairs.

followups.q: Why does the loop run to cost.Length inclusive?
followups.a: Because the destination is the floor above the last step, which is index cost.Length in the conceptual array of positions. Stopping at cost.Length - 1 would compute the cost of standing on the last step rather than of finishing the climb, and would give the wrong answer whenever stepping over the last stair is cheaper. The [5,5] case shows it: the answer is 5, reached by starting at index 1 and stepping past the top, not 10.

followups.q: Why do both starting positions cost zero?
followups.a: Because the problem says you may begin on either step 0 or step 1 without paying to arrive there - you pay only when you leave a step. So the two seed values are both 0, and the first real cost is incurred at index 2. Seeding with the step costs instead would double-charge the starting step, which gives an answer that is too large by exactly cost[0] or cost[1] and is easy to miss on symmetric test data.

followups.q: How is this different from the plain climbing-stairs problem?
followups.a: That one counts the number of ways and this one minimises a cost, so the operator changes from addition to minimum-plus-weight while the recurrence shape is identical. Recognising that a whole family - climbing stairs, min cost climbing stairs, house robber, and the coin-change variants - is one recurrence with a different combining operator is worth far more than memorising four solutions, and interviewers often ask two of them in sequence to see whether you notice.

question: Delete and earn: earning a number deletes all copies of its neighbours.

followups.q: Why aggregate by value before applying the DP?
followups.a: Because taking a value takes every copy of it in one action, so the decision is per distinct value rather than per element. Aggregating turns 'three 3s' into a single choice worth 9, which is what the recurrence needs. Without it you would be deciding about individual elements that are not independent, and the no-two-adjacent rule would not apply cleanly. The aggregation is the step that makes the reduction valid.

followups.q: Why iterate the value range rather than the distinct values present?
followups.a: Because the adjacency constraint is about numeric neighbours, so a missing value must still occupy a position in the walk - it contributes zero but it breaks the adjacency between the values either side. The [2,2,3,3,3,4,9] case shows why: 9 is far from the rest, so taking it costs nothing elsewhere. Iterating only the present values would wrongly treat 4 and 9 as adjacent. The trade is memory proportional to the maximum value, which a sorted-distinct-values version with an explicit gap check avoids.

followups.q: What if the values were very large or sparse?
followups.a: The points array becomes impractical - a single value of a billion would allocate a billion entries. The fix is to sort the distinct values and run the same recurrence over that list, checking explicitly whether each value is exactly one more than the previous: if so apply the adjacency rule, otherwise both options are free. That is O(n log n) and uses memory proportional to the distinct count, which is the right version whenever the value range is not small.

question: Longest string chain: longest sequence where each word is a predecessor of the next.

followups.q: Why generate predecessors by deletion rather than comparing every pair?
followups.a: Because a word of length L has exactly L possible predecessors, which you can enumerate and look up in constant time each. Comparing against every other word is O(n) per word and each comparison costs O(L) to verify the one-deletion relationship, giving O(n squared L). Generating is O(L squared) per word including the string construction, which for realistic word lengths is dramatically smaller. It is the same generate-versus-compare choice as in word ladder.

followups.q: Why does sorting by length suffice, without sorting alphabetically?
followups.a: Because a predecessor is always exactly one character shorter, so length order alone guarantees it has been processed. Alphabetical order is irrelevant to the dependency. Contrast the longest-buildable-word problem, where the alphabetical tie-break matters because the answer must be lexicographically smallest - here only the chain length is wanted, so no tie-break is needed at all.

followups.q: What if a chain could skip more than one character?
followups.a: The predecessor generation would explode: allowing two deletions gives L choose 2 candidates per word, and allowing any number gives all subsequences, which is exponential. At that point the problem becomes a longest-path search over a subsequence relation, and you would compare pairs with a subsequence check instead, at O(n squared L). The one-character restriction is what keeps the generate-and-lookup approach viable, which is worth stating rather than assuming.

question: Count square submatrices with all ones.

followups.q: Why does the cell's value equal the number of squares ending there?
followups.a: Because if the largest square with that bottom-right corner has side k, then squares of side 1 through k all also end at that cell, and no larger one does - that is exactly k squares. Every square in the matrix has exactly one bottom-right corner, so summing over all cells counts each square once with no double counting. That bijection between squares and (corner, side) pairs is the whole argument.

followups.q: Why the minimum of three neighbours rather than two?
followups.a: Because a square of side k needs squares of side k-1 to exist above, to the left, and diagonally. Using only two would let an L-shaped region count as a square: a full row and column meeting at a corner with a hole between them. The diagonal neighbour certifies the interior is solid. Dropping it is the standard error and it passes every test whose ones form solid rectangles, which is most casual test data.

followups.q: The code modifies the caller's matrix. Would you ship that?
followups.a: It saves allocating a second grid, which for a large matrix is real, but it destroys the input - a caller reusing the matrix afterwards sees side lengths where it expected zeros and ones. For an interview it is worth naming as a deliberate trade. In production I would either allocate a DP array, or reduce to a single rolling row since each cell only needs the previous row, which is O(cols) rather than O(rows x cols) and leaves the input alone.

question: Minimum falling path sum through a matrix.

followups.q: Why take the minimum of the whole final row rather than the last cell?
followups.a: Because the path starts anywhere in the top row and ends anywhere in the bottom row - it is not required to finish in a particular column. Returning the last cell would answer a different question, namely the cheapest path ending at the bottom-right, and would give a larger answer whenever a better path exits elsewhere. The [100,1] / [1,100] case makes it visible: the answer 2 comes from starting at column 1 and moving diagonally, ending at column 0.

followups.q: Why clone the first row rather than using it directly?
followups.a: Because writing into it would modify the caller's matrix, and the algorithm reads matrix[r][c] for the current row's own values while building the new totals. Cloning costs one row of memory and keeps the input intact. The alternative of computing in place is possible if mutation is acceptable and saves the allocation, which is the same trade as in count-square-submatrices - worth making explicitly rather than by accident.

followups.q: How does this differ from minimum path sum in a grid?
followups.a: That problem allows only right and down moves, so a cell has two predecessors and the path must run corner to corner. Here the movement is downward with a diagonal drift, so there are three predecessors and both endpoints are free. The recurrence shape is the same but the neighbour set and the answer extraction differ, which is a good illustration that grid DPs are distinguished by their move set rather than by being 'grid problems'.

question: Triangle: minimum path sum from top to bottom moving to adjacent numbers.

followups.q: Why is bottom-up simpler than top-down here?
followups.a: Because going upward every cell has exactly two children - the row below is always one element longer - so no bounds checks are needed. Going downward, a cell's parents are one or two depending on whether it is at an edge, which needs conditionals at both ends of every row. The answer also lands in a single cell rather than requiring a minimum over the last row. It is a case where the direction of the DP changes the amount of code substantially.

followups.q: Why is the array one longer than the triangle's height?
followups.a: So that best[col + 1] is always a valid index on the first iteration, when col can reach the last row's final position. The extra entry stays zero and acts as a sentinel that never wins a minimum against real values, provided the bottom row is written first - which it is, since the loop starts there. It is the same padding trick as in maximal-square, adding an element so the general rule covers the boundary.

followups.q: Can it be done in O(1) extra space?
followups.a: Yes, by writing the sums back into the triangle itself, which the problem sometimes permits. That mutates the caller's data, which is the usual objection. The O(n) rolling row is a good compromise: it is proportional to the triangle's height rather than its area, so for a triangle of a thousand rows it is a thousand integers against half a million cells, and the input is left alone.

question: Dungeon game: minimum initial health to reach the bottom-right alive.

followups.q: Why does a forward DP fail?
followups.a: Because two objectives conflict and neither dominates. Tracking maximum accumulated health picks a route that may dip below zero somewhere along the way; tracking minimum requirement forward needs to know what lies ahead, which a forward pass does not have. A cell's value cannot be evaluated without knowing the rest of the path, so the subproblems are not independent in that direction. Reversing makes them independent, because the requirement at a cell depends only on cells already solved.

followups.q: Why floor the requirement at 1?
followups.a: Because health must stay strictly positive at all times, so even after a large potion the requirement on entering the next cell cannot drop to zero or below. Without the floor, a cell containing 100 would propagate a negative requirement backwards and the final answer could come out as zero or negative, which is not a valid starting health. The single-cell test with 100 confirms the answer is 1 rather than a negative number.

followups.q: Why is the padding initialised to int.MaxValue rather than zero?
followups.a: So that out-of-bounds directions never win the minimum against a real neighbour. Zero would make every edge cell believe it can exit freely in the wrong direction, producing requirements that are far too low. The two genuine exits just past the bottom-right are set to 1 explicitly, which is the only place the padding should be permissive. It is an in-band sentinel and it works because a real requirement can never reach int.MaxValue.

question: Count palindromic substrings in a string.

followups.q: Why are there 2n-1 centres rather than n?
followups.a: Because an even-length palindrome has its centre between two characters rather than on one. With n characters there are n single-character centres and n-1 gaps, giving 2n-1 in total. Checking only the n character centres misses every even-length palindrome, so 'aa' would not be counted and 'aaa' would report 3 instead of 6. It is the same omission that breaks the longest-palindromic-substring problem, and the two questions are usually asked together.

followups.q: Why does every successful expansion count as one palindrome?
followups.a: Because expanding from a centre produces a strictly longer palindrome at each step, and each is a distinct substring. So the number of successful steps is the number of palindromes with that centre. Since every palindrome has exactly one centre, summing across all centres counts each substring once with no duplicates. That bijection is what makes the counting correct without any deduplication.

followups.q: Why does aaaa give 10?
followups.a: Because every substring of a string of identical characters is a palindrome, and a string of length n has n(n+1)/2 substrings, which is 10 for n of 4. That is the worst case for this algorithm, since every expansion runs to the full width, giving the O(n squared) bound. It is a useful test precisely because it exercises the maximum work and confirms the count formula rather than a coincidence.

question: Russian doll envelopes: maximum number of nested envelopes.

followups.q: Why must heights be sorted descending within equal widths?
followups.a: Because envelopes of equal width cannot nest, so at most one of them may appear in the answer. Descending heights make them a strictly decreasing run, and a strictly increasing subsequence can take only one element from such a run - the sort enforces the constraint for free. With ascending heights, [3,1] and [3,9] look like an increasing pair and the answer comes out as 2 instead of 1, which is exactly what the last test checks.

followups.q: What does the tails array actually hold?
followups.a: tails[i] is the smallest possible tail value among all increasing subsequences of length i+1 seen so far. It is not itself a valid subsequence - the values may come from positions that do not form one - but its length is always the LIS length, and keeping the tails minimal is what lets a longer subsequence be extended later. Confusing the array with the answer subsequence is the usual misunderstanding; reconstructing the actual envelopes needs a separate predecessor array.

followups.q: Why binary search for the first element not less than the height?
followups.a: Because we want strictly increasing nesting, so a tail equal to the current height must be replaced rather than extended past. Searching for the first element greater than or equal to the height, and overwriting it, gives strict increase. If the problem allowed equal dimensions to nest, the search would move to the first strictly greater element instead. That one comparison boundary is the difference between the strict and non-strict variants of every LIS problem.

question: Interleaving string: is s3 formed by interleaving s1 and s2?

followups.q: Why does a greedy two-pointer approach fail?
followups.a: Because when s3's next character matches the head of both s1 and s2, the choice is not locally decidable - one branch may dead-end many characters later. Greedy would have to backtrack, which is exponential in the worst case. The DP records reachability for every prefix pair, so both branches are explored once and shared. It is the same reason greedy fails on wildcard matching and succeeds on jump game: the difference is whether a local choice can be proved safe.

followups.q: In the rolling row, why is row[j] the previous row while row[j-1] is the current one?
followups.a: Because the inner loop writes left to right, so by the time index j is computed, index j-1 has already been overwritten with the current row's value while index j still holds the previous row's. That is exactly what the recurrence needs - coming from s1 uses the cell above, coming from s2 uses the cell to the left. Getting the iteration direction wrong silently reads the wrong generation, which is the classic rolling-array bug.

followups.q: Why check the lengths first?
followups.a: Because an interleaving uses every character of both strings exactly once, so the combined length is forced - if it does not match, no arrangement can work and the answer is false regardless of content. It is also a safety property: without it, s3[i + j - 1] could index past the end. So the check is both an O(1) early exit on a common failing input and the guard that makes the indexing provably in range.

question: Minimum insertions to make a string a palindrome.

followups.q: Why is the answer n minus the longest palindromic subsequence?
followups.a: Because the characters in that subsequence are already correctly paired around the centre and need nothing added, while every other character is unpaired and needs exactly one insertion to mirror it. No insertion can fix two unpaired characters at once, and no fewer insertions can work, so the count is exactly the number of characters outside the subsequence. That both-directions argument is what makes it a proof rather than an observation.

followups.q: Why does LCS with the reverse give the longest palindromic subsequence?
followups.a: Because a palindromic subsequence of s reads identically forwards and backwards, so it is also a subsequence of the reversed string - hence a common subsequence. Conversely any common subsequence of s and its reverse can be shown to be palindromic. The two quantities coincide, which lets you reuse the standard LCS table instead of deriving a separate recurrence. It is a good reduction to know because it also solves 'minimum deletions to make a palindrome', which is the same number.

followups.q: Why do the two rows get swapped rather than copied?
followups.a: Because copying an array of n+1 integers every iteration adds an O(n squared) memory traffic cost for no benefit, whereas swapping the references is constant time. The tuple swap makes the intent obvious in one line. The subtlety is that the array that becomes 'current' still holds stale values from two rows back, which is safe here only because every entry is written before it is read - if the inner loop ever skipped an index, it would read garbage.

question: Paint house: minimum cost to paint houses so no two adjacent share a colour.

followups.q: Why keep three totals rather than one running minimum?
followups.a: Because the adjacency rule is about which colour the previous house used, so the cheapest total overall is useless if it happens to end in the colour you now want. Keeping the best total per ending colour lets you exclude exactly the forbidden one. The [1,100,100] twice case shows it: the cheapest first house is red at 1, but the second house cannot also be red, so the answer is 101 rather than 2.

followups.q: Why compute all three before assigning any?
followups.a: Because each new total reads all three old totals, so assigning red first would make blue and green read the already-updated value and silently allow two adjacent reds. The three temporaries enforce that the whole row is computed from the previous generation. It is the same simultaneity requirement as in Conway's life or any in-place DP over a fixed-size state, and overwriting early is the bug that hides until a specific cost pattern exposes it.

followups.q: How would you extend this to k colours?
followups.a: Naively you would take the minimum over the other k-1 colours for each of k colours, which is O(n k squared). The fix is to track the smallest and second-smallest totals from the previous house along with which colour achieved the smallest: for any colour, the best other total is the smallest unless that smallest is this very colour, in which case it is the second smallest. That makes it O(n k), and it is exactly what the paint-house-II follow-up asks for.

question: Integer break: maximise the product of integers summing to n.

followups.q: Why does the recurrence need both total - part and best[total - part]?
followups.a: Because the remainder is sometimes better left as a single number than split further. For n of 4 the answer is 2 times 2, but for n of 3 the best is 3 itself taken whole - and best[3] is 2, since the DP definition forces at least one split. Taking only best[total - part] would apply that forced split to the remainder too and undercount. The maximum of the two covers both readings of the subproblem.

followups.q: Why are threes optimal, and why is a remainder of 1 special?
followups.a: Because for a fixed sum, 3 times 3 is 9 while 2 times 2 times 2 is 8, so threes pack more product per unit of sum than twos, and anything 5 or larger beats itself by splitting off a 3. A remainder of 1 is wasteful because multiplying by 1 adds nothing: 3 plus 1 gives a product of 3, whereas regrouping as 2 plus 2 gives 4. The loop stopping at n greater than 4 handles that by leaving 4 as two 2s rather than 3 and 1.

followups.q: Why does the maths version return n - 1 for n up to 3?
followups.a: Because the problem requires at least two parts, so 2 must become 1 plus 1 with a product of 1, and 3 must become 1 plus 2 with a product of 2 - both n - 1. Without that forced split the answer would trivially be n itself. It is the base case where the greedy formula would otherwise return the number unbroken, and it is the case most people get wrong when they jump straight to the closed form.

question: Minimum cost for tickets given travel days and daily, weekly and monthly passes.

followups.q: Why index the calendar rather than the travel days?
followups.a: Because a 7-day pass covers seven consecutive calendar days regardless of how many of them involve travel, so the lookback must be in days. Indexing by travel position would make the pass duration depend on how spread out the trips are, which is not expressible as a fixed offset. The cost is an array as long as the last travel day rather than as long as the trip list - acceptable for a year, and if the days were huge you would switch to a map keyed by travel day with a binary search for the lookback.

followups.q: Why clamp the lookback with Math.Max(0, ...)?
followups.a: Because a 30-day pass bought on day 5 covers everything from before the calendar began, so the correct predecessor is day 0 with cost zero, not a negative index. The clamp expresses 'nothing was needed before the start'. Without it you get an index-out-of-range on any trip in the first 29 days, which is most small test cases - it is the first thing that breaks if you write the recurrence without thinking about the boundary.

followups.q: Why can a greedy rule not solve this?
followups.a: Because buying the pass that covers the most upcoming travel days is not always right - a cheap 7-day pass may cover three trips where a 30-day pass covering eight trips is better value per trip, and which wins depends on what comes after. The DP tries all three at every travel day and lets the accumulated cost decide. It is the same reason coin change needs DP for arbitrary denominations: local best-value does not compose into a global optimum.

question: Design a browser history with back, forward and visit.

followups.q: Why a list with an index rather than two stacks?
followups.a: Two stacks work, with back and forward stacks exchanging entries, but visiting a page must then clear the entire forward stack, and moving several steps at once means popping and pushing repeatedly rather than a single index arithmetic. The list version makes a multi-step move O(1) and truncation a single RemoveRange. The stack version is arguably more intuitive to describe, so it is worth mentioning, but the index version is cleaner to implement.

followups.q: Why clamp rather than throw when there are not enough steps?
followups.a: Because it matches what a browser does: holding the back button past the start of history simply stops at the first page. Throwing would force every caller into a try/catch for an entirely normal situation. It is the same reasoning as returning 0 profit for an empty price array. Where the distinction matters, a method returning how many steps were actually taken would let a caller detect the clamp without exceptions.

followups.q: RemoveRange is O(n). Does that matter?
followups.a: Rarely, because it only runs when visiting after going back, and it removes entries that are being discarded anyway. The worst case is a long forward history discarded repeatedly, which is unusual behaviour. If it did matter, you would keep a logical end index rather than physically truncating, treating entries beyond it as invisible, which makes Visit O(1) at the cost of not releasing the discarded strings for garbage collection.

followups.q: What would a real browser need beyond this?
followups.a: Per-tab history, since each tab has its own stack, plus session restore, which means persisting it. Entries carry scroll position and form state, not just a URL. Back and forward interact with the page cache, which is why going back is often instant. And redirects must not create extra history entries, or the back button would bounce the user through a redirect chain, which is a classic bug in single-page applications that push state manually.

question: Design an underground system tracking average travel time between stations.

followups.q: Why store a running total rather than every journey time?
followups.a: Because the total and count give the average in O(1) with two fields per route, whereas a list grows without bound and would eventually exhaust memory on a busy network. The trade-off is that you can no longer compute anything the running aggregate does not capture: percentiles, the median, or the distribution. If those were needed you would keep a histogram of bucketed durations, which is still bounded, or a t-digest for approximate quantiles.

followups.q: Is the route key of concatenated strings a problem?
followups.a: It is a small one. Building a string on every checkout allocates, and if a station name could contain the separator the key would be ambiguous. A tuple key, `(string, string)`, avoids both: .NET value tuples have structural equality and hashing, so they work directly as dictionary keys with no allocation for the key itself. I would use a tuple in production and would mention that the string concatenation is a shortcut.

followups.q: What happens if a passenger never checks out?
followups.a: Their entry stays in the travelling map forever, which is a slow memory leak and, in a real system, an unresolved fare. Transport networks handle this with a maximum journey time after which the entry is expired and a penalty fare is charged. Here you would sweep entries older than some threshold, or store an expiry alongside the entry and clean lazily on access. It is worth raising unprompted, because the happy path hides it entirely.

followups.q: Why does the code throw on a double check-in rather than overwriting?
followups.a: Because a card checking in twice without checking out means either a hardware fault or fare evasion, and silently overwriting would discard the first journey and hide the problem. Failing loudly surfaces it. That said, in a real system throwing at the barrier is unacceptable, so you would log and apply a business rule instead. The general point is that the data structure should not paper over an inconsistency it has detected.

question: Design a data structure supporting insert, delete, getRandom and duplicates.

followups.q: Why is the index == lastIndex case special?
followups.a: Because when the element being removed is already at the end, there is nothing to swap, and performing the swap logic anyway would re-add `index` to the moved value's set even though that slot is about to be trimmed away. The set would then contain a dangling index pointing past the end of the list, and a later operation would read or write out of bounds. Guarding the swap is the fix, and this case is the single most common bug in the duplicate-supporting version.

followups.q: Does GetRandom return each distinct value with equal probability?
followups.a: No, and that is usually the desired behaviour.
